Anxiety has become a constant companion in my life. I constantly worry about everything - from small everyday tasks to major life decisions. My heart races, palms sweat, and sometimes I even have trouble breathing when these anxious thoughts take over.

It can be challenging to live with constant anxiety, where worries seem to infiltrate every aspect of your life. The physical symptoms you described, such as a racing heart, sweaty palms, and difficulty breathing, are common manifestations of anxiety. It's important to remember that you're not alone in experiencing these feelings.

One suggestion I have is to try incorporating relaxation techniques into your daily routine. Deep breathing exercises, for example, can help calm your body and mind when anxiety starts to take hold. Taking slow, deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth can activate the body's relaxation response and reduce some of the physical symptoms you mentioned.

Another strategy that may be helpful is practicing mindfulness. Mindfulness involves focusing on the present moment without judgment or attachment to thoughts or emotions. By cultivating awareness of your thoughts and redirecting your attention to the present, you can potentially lessen the impact of anxious thoughts on your overall well-being.

Engaging in regular physical activity can also be beneficial for managing anxiety. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Finding an activity that you enjoy, whether it's going for a walk, dancing, or participating in a sport, can provide a healthy outlet for stress and anxiety.

Additionally, it might be worth exploring any underlying causes or triggers for your anxiety. Reflecting on past experiences or situations that may have contributed to your current state can offer valuable insights. If certain patterns or themes emerge, you could consider seeking support from a mental health professional who can guide you through this process and provide personalized strategies for coping with anxiety.

Remember, finding what works best for you may involve some trial and error. Be patient with yourself as you explore different techniques and approaches. And always remember that there is hope for managing and reducing anxiety so that it doesn't dominate your life.

I know someone who is extremely sensitive to stress and very sensitive to a negative tone of voice. Sometimes during a disagreement he tells me that my communication is having a harmful impact on him. Once he believes I am being negative I can't seem to find a better way of communicating. In fact, it is often a self fulling prophesy because his accusatory manner becomes unbearably frustrating. 

What advice might you offer?

With any type of criticism, it is usually best to introduce the topic at a neutral time, ie: when both of you are relaxed, with no current stressors involved, having fun, etc.  Begin with a non-judgmental reflective comment about a recent bothersome event, as if it were just then crossing your mind (therefore not something you've been consumed with ruminating over - eases the impulse for him to dive straight into defense mode).Then share how you felt at the time of the event.  Just say when.... I felt kind of hurt / shocked (or whatever the feeling was).  PERIOD.  THATS ALL YOU SHOULD SAY.  Wait for him to respond to your matter-of-fact statement.No matter what his response is, stick to your same message - don't get overwhelmed by trying to rephrase or explain your view as that will likely set you up for continued arguing.  You can even add, "I agree I could have misunderstood  it (event).... I just know it made me feel uneasy."Here you give him little wiggle room for a debate.Good luck & I'd love to hear how it goes!

Lately, I've been experiencing intense anxiety whenever I'm in crowded places. It feels like everyone is watching me, judging my every move. I start sweating profusely, my heart races, and it becomes difficult to breathe. I hope through counseling, I can learn techniques to cope with my anxiety and overcome these overwhelming feelings.

In situations where you experience intense anxiety in crowded places, it can be helpful to have strategies in place to cope with these overwhelming feelings. While I am not a mental health professional or counselor, here are some suggestions to consider:

1. Deep Breathing Techniques: Learning deep breathing exercises can help you regulate your breath and calm your body during moments of heightened anxiety. Practice taking slow, deep breaths in through your nose, allowing your abdomen to expand, and exhaling slowly through your mouth.

2. Grounding Techniques: Utilize grounding techniques to bring yourself back to the present moment. Focus on your senses by identifying five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

3. Cognitive Behavioral Strategies: Challenge negative thoughts that may contribute to your anxiety in crowded places. Ask yourself if there is evidence to support the belief that everyone is watching and judging you. Try replacing unhelpful thoughts with more balanced and realistic ones.

4. Gradual Exposure: Consider gradually exposing yourself to increasing levels of crowded spaces over time. Start with smaller gatherings or less busy environments and work your way up to larger crowds. This approach allows you to build confidence and develop coping skills at a pace that feels manageable for you.

5. Self-Care Practices: Engage in self-care activities that promote overall well-being and reduce stress. This might include making time for hobbies you enjoy, getting regular exercise, maintaining a healthy diet, ensuring adequate sleep, and practicing relaxation techniques such as mindfulness or meditation.

6. Seeking Support: If your anxiety continues to significantly impact your daily life, don't hesitate to reach out to qualified mental health professionals who can provide additional guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember that every individual's experiences and preferences may vary, so it can be beneficial to explore what works best for you in managing your anxiety. Take it one step at a time, be patient with yourself, and celebrate the progress you make along the way.

Being a parent has been incredibly challenging for me. I love my children more than anything, but sometimes I feel overwhelmed and unsure if I'm doing the right thing. I constantly worry about their well-being and whether I'm providing them with enough support and guidance. How can I be a better parent and ensure their happiness?

Parenting can definitely be challenging, and it's completely normal to feel overwhelmed at times. It's clear that you deeply care about your children and want the best for them, which is a wonderful quality in a parent.

To become a better parent and ensure their happiness, here are a few suggestions:

1. Take care of yourself: Remember that self-care is crucial. When you prioritize your own well-being, you'll have more energy and patience to give to your children. Make sure to get enough rest, eat nutritious meals, engage in activities you enjoy, and seek support from friends or family when needed.

2. Communication is key: Open and honest communication with your children is essential. Encourage them to express their thoughts and feelings, and actively listen without judgment. This will help build trust and strengthen your relationship with them.

3. Set boundaries and routines: Children thrive on structure and consistency. Establish clear rules and expectations, and consistently enforce them. Having predictable routines can provide a sense of security and stability for both you and your children.

4. Show love and affection: Express your love and affection regularly. Hugs, kisses, and kind words can go a long way in making your children feel valued and secure. Celebrate their achievements, no matter how small, and let them know they are loved unconditionally.

5. Foster independence: As parents, we naturally want to protect our children, but it's important to also encourage their independence. Allow them age-appropriate responsibilities and decision-making opportunities. This helps build their confidence and prepares them for adulthood.

6. Seek support: Remember that you don't have to do this alone. Reach out to other parents, join parenting groups, or participate in community programs where you can connect with others who may be going through similar experiences. Sharing ideas and seeking advice from those who understand can be incredibly helpful.

Remember, every parent makes mistakes along the way, and that's okay. What matters most is that you're there for your children, providing love, support, and guidance to the best of your abilities. Trust yourself and have faith in your instincts as a parent. You're doing great!

What should I not do if I see a bear?

Everyone knows that bears are not fluffy friends, and are unfortunately likely to maul humans. There is clear guidance on what to do depending on what type of bear you see: if it’s a black bear, make yourself loud and fight if necessary. If it’s a brown bear, lay down and cover your head. If it’s a polar bear, hope you updated your will recently. However, there is very little guidance on what not to do if you see a bear. Thankfully it is easy to provide guidance that applies to all bear types. First, do not attempt to hug the bear. While they do look fluffy and very much in need of a hug, bears highly value consent and will attempt to eat you if you ignore that. Next, do not invite a bear over for dinner. While some bears, black bears especially, may look like good dinner guests they are known for extremely rude eating habits and will likely dirty your house. Further, some types of bears might think that you are the menu. It is also not a good idea to challenge a bear to a game of basketball. Most bears are actually extremely adept at basketball, and this would likely hurt your ego considerably as they would dunk on you and then eat you as a celebration for winning. While this is not an exhaustive list of what not to do if you see a bear, it covers the most common questions.
I know I need to deal with my depression. But I don't know how and I don't want to tell anyone.    How can I deal with depression without telling anyone?

Hello,It is completely understandable that you would not want people to know about your depression. I would first like commend you for realizing that you need to help with your depression by reaching out here. That is a great start, and you've taken the very first courageous step. Depression can feel debilitating and overwhelming. Depression is also a very personal thing and no one has know but you and the therapist. The best way to begin learningand dealing is to pick up the phone and call a therapist or email a therapist and schedule a session. The great news is that with professional help you can feel better and you will learn how deal with and manage the depression. There are many ways to help with depression that a therapist can teach you and help guide. You do not have do this alone. Asking for help and going to therapy is a strength! This can be done in a private and confidential setting.Depression should be treated by a therapist, in a safe, confidential office setting. The therapist can then discuss your depression with you in more detail to figure out the underlying cause, how long you've been feeling this way and identify what brings on these feelings. There is hope and depression can be treated with great success, you CAN feel good again. Depression can be managed appropriately by seeing a licensed therapist. Often times therapy will offer relief because you would have someone there simply to listen to you, validate your feelings and listen to your story. The therapist will be able to offer professional insight and perspective on the situation and help you think outside the box. The therapist can do many things with you, provide insight and offer many ideas to help you learn new coping skills and ideas of things you enjoy, encouraging you to re engage in hobbies you once enjoyed or even discover new things you may enjoy. There are creative ways to learn to cope too!Your therapist will also be there to support you, without judgement, at your pace, through the entire process. But the first step is finding a therapist and beginning to identify the cause your depression. Healing is possible and getting your happiness back is also possible.Feel free contact me for additional help or informationLaura Cassity, LMSW, LMAC

It's important to acknowledge the intensity of your anxiety symptoms and how they are impacting you. When experiencing racing thoughts, a rapid heartbeat, and difficulty breathing, it can feel incredibly overwhelming.

One technique that may help is deep breathing exercises. These can be done anytime, anywhere, and can provide immediate relief in moments of anxiety. You can try inhaling deeply through your nose for a count of four, holding your breath for a count of four, and exhaling slowly through your mouth for a count of eight. This type of controlled breathing can help calm your body's stress response.

Another strategy to consider is mindfulness meditation. Mindfulness involves focusing on the present moment without judgment, allowing us to observe our thoughts and feelings as they arise and pass. By practicing regular mindfulness, you can gain a better understanding of your anxiety triggers and develop increased self-awareness.

In addition to these techniques, it could be helpful to gradually expose yourself to situations that trigger your anxiety. Gradual exposure allows you to face your fears in a structured way, starting with less challenging situations and working your way up to more difficult ones. Over time, this process can reduce the intensity of your anxiety response and increase your sense of control.

Remember to prioritize self-care activities in your daily routine as well. Engaging in activities that bring you joy, relaxation, or a sense of accomplishment can serve as a buffer against anxiety. This might include hobbies, exercise, spending time in nature, connecting with supportive friends or family members, or engaging in creative outlets such as writing or art.

Lastly, seeking guidance from a professional mental health therapist who specializes in anxiety can offer valuable strategies tailored specifically to your needs. They can provide additional support, tools, and techniques to help you manage your anxiety more effectively.

"There has been ongoing conflict between my parents, and I often find myself caught in the middle. The tension at home affects my mental well-being and overall happiness. I really need guidance on how to navigate the familial conflicts and establish healthy boundaries."

Conflicts within the family can be incredibly challenging and impactful on one's mental well-being. It is understandable that you feel caught in the middle, as it can bring about feelings of stress and emotional burden. To navigate these familial conflicts and establish healthy boundaries, here are some suggestions:

1. Self-care: Prioritize your own self-care to ensure you have the strength and resilience to handle these conflicts. Engage in activities that bring you joy and peace, such as spending time with friends or pursuing hobbies.

2. Emotion regulation: When conflicts arise, it can be easy to get overwhelmed by emotions. Practice deep breathing exercises, mindfulness, or other techniques that help you stay calm and centered during tense situations.

3. Communicate openly: Try to express your thoughts and feelings to both of your parents separately and listen to their perspectives without judgment. Let them know how the ongoing conflicts affect you personally.

4. Neutral ground: Encourage your parents to have constructive conversations in a neutral setting where everyone feels safe and heard. Suggest that they focus on finding resolutions rather than fueling the conflicts further.

5. Set boundaries: Clearly communicate your boundaries and expectations to your parents regarding their conflicts and involvement from both sides. Explain what you are comfortable with and what you need to maintain your mental well-being.

6. Seek support: Reach out to trusted friends or relatives who can provide emotional support and guidance during these challenging times. Sometimes talking to someone outside the situation can offer new perspectives and helpful advice.

7. Write down your thoughts: Consider keeping a journal to process your feelings and thoughts about the ongoing conflicts. Writing things down can help you gain clarity and understand your own needs better.

8. Educate yourself: Read books or articles about conflict resolution strategies, effective communication, and establishing healthy boundaries within families. This knowledge may equip you with additional tools and insights for navigating these challenges.

Remember, navigating familial conflicts takes time, effort, and patience. You are not responsible for resolving your parents' issues, but you can prioritize your own well-being by implementing these suggestions. Practice self-compassion throughout this process, as it can be difficult at times. If needed, don't hesitate to reach out to mental health professionals who can provide further guidance tailored to your specific situation.

My mother takes care of niece whom my sister abandoned. She calls me every day complaining, but I don't want to hear it anymore.

It is understandable that it's very hard for you to hear daily complaints from your mother regarding the caregiving of your niece. You cannot change your mother's feelings and responsibilities, which could create feelings of frustration and helplessness. It must be equally hard for your mother to assume full responsibility for your niece at a time where your sister cannot take care of her. This type of responsibility usually produces an enormous amount of stress and pressure because your mother and niece would both need to adapt to this new relationship, living situation, and the feeling of being "abandoned." Not knowing the history of your relationship with your mother and how you respond to each other in times of need, it may be difficult to fight the right recommendation on how to deal with this situation. Nonetheless, it is not easy to have to face daily complaints and you may have to set a healthy balance between empathy and boundary setting with your mother and some personal boundaries for yourself. It is likely that your mother's "complaints" may be her desperate cry for help because she does not know how to cope with stress or how to ask for the right kind of support. In this case, you could calmly and respectfully tell her the next time you hear her complain, "This must be very difficult for you because I hear the stress in your voice almost everyday. It's very hard for me to hear you feeling so overwhelmed. I feel helpless in this situation and would like to suggest that it might be helpful for you to seek some professional help and support to deal with such a big matter of importance." When empathy and understanding is communicated, recipients are usually more open because they hear and feel the caring behind it and are more likely to seek additional help.After sharing this message of empathy and encouragement to seek help, the next step is to protect yourself by explaining to your mother where your limits are so that she understands what she can expect from you. This means that you can decide the kind of support or help you are willing to give your mother and/or niece that is within your ability to provide without feeling overwhelmed. This could involve inviting them to dinner occasionally, taking them out to see a movie or inviting your niece over to give your mother respite. You could then say to her if she complains again, "I cannot change the way you feel in this situation and I encourage you to seek professional advice about that but what I could do is .........(explain what you could do to help)."www.PsychologyResource.ca

What makes a healthy marriage last?

What a great question! Marriage (or any long-term committed romantic relationship) is never easy. Ups & downs, doubts and fights are a part of it just the same as the wonderful, tender, blissful moments of connection. Recognizing that hardships are normal and something to work through is a big part of the healthy attitude partners in lasting relationships share. Some degree of conflict is not something to be scared of or a sign it's time to break up as long as all parties involved feel respected. Expressing your needs and wants in a respectful, not accusing manner will increase the chances that your loved one will actually listen, empathize with your perspective and will be more open to finding solutions to your problems together. Working as a team to find solutions to problems you encounter is a much better approach than trying to persuade your partner that you are right, while they are most certainly wrong. Shutting your partner out or allowing resentment and contempt to creep into your relationships is definitely a warning sign that things may not be going the way you want anymore. As long as you both agree that you want to be in that relationship (i.e., are committed to it) and you have a growth mindset ("we will learn from this and grow together to be a better couple in the end"), the foundation of your partnership is strong. What else? Making time for each other, whether it's being playful, having fun or enjoying intimate moments together is also an important part of ensuring a good balance of positive to negative experiences, that will only strenghten your bond. Good luck!

"I can't stop blaming myself for what happened to me. I keep replaying the events in my head, wondering if there was something I could have done differently. This guilt and self-blame consume me, making it difficult to trust others and feel safe. Through counseling, I hope to shift this mindset and embark on a journey of healing and self-forgiveness."

It's understandable that you're struggling with self-blame and guilt related to your past trauma. It can be challenging to let go of those thoughts and feelings, but it is possible to work towards healing and self-forgiveness. 

One strategy that might help is practicing self-compassion. Instead of blaming yourself, try to treat yourself with the kindness and understanding you would offer to a friend who has experienced something similar. Remind yourself that you did the best you could in the circumstances, and acknowledge that no one is responsible for traumatic events happening to them.

Another approach that may be helpful is reframing your perspective. Ask yourself if there might be alternative ways to view the situation that are more forgiving towards yourself. Consider seeking support from trusted individuals, such as close friends or family members, who can provide an outside perspective and remind you of your worth.

Engaging in activities that promote relaxation and stress reduction, such as meditation, deep breathing exercises, or yoga, could also be beneficial. These practices can aid in grounding yourself in the present moment and reducing rumination on the past.

In addition, consider exploring therapeutic techniques like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) with a licensed mental health professional when you feel ready. CBT can help you challenge negative thoughts and replace them with healthier and more constructive ones. Ultimately, working through these emotions takes time and patience, so remember to be gentle with yourself throughout this process. Keep in mind that everyone's healing journey is unique, and what works for others may not necessarily work for you.

Remember, you are deserving of healing and self-forgiveness. By taking steps to address these negative feelings and seeking support, you can gradually shift your mindset and find a path towards healing and peace.

Are you facing any type of overwhelming situation in your waking life?Dreams and nightmares are the non-logical ways in which we make emotional sense of what goes on in our everyday waking world.Besides having some type of relaxing bedtime routine to set a peaceful mood for your sleep, and avoiding viewing violent films and video games as entertainment, maybe even avoiding news stories which sometimes have similar themes of violence, the content of our dreams and nightmares is out of our direct control.Your nightmares may offer useful clues as to what you're trying to resolve in your life.  Pay attention to the story of your nightmare because it reflects how you feel in waking life.If you feel helpless and silenced in your nightmare, or taken advantage of, or whatever dreadful situation goes on during your nightmare, then look for where in waking life, you may feel similar.In this way, you'll become clearer about stressors in your life that you may not have realized existed were it not for the stress of nightmares.

Getting out of a maze can be a challenging task, but with a few tips and strategies, it can be accomplished. Here are some steps to follow to help you get out of a maze:

Stay Calm and Focused: Getting lost in a maze can be frustrating, but it's important to stay calm and focused. Take deep breaths, relax, and clear your mind. This will help you to think more clearly and make better decisions.

Plan Your Route: Take a few minutes to look at the maze from above, if possible, and try to identify the route to the exit. Identify landmarks or walls that you can use as reference points. Look for any dead ends, and try to avoid them.

Follow One Wall: If you can't identify the exit route, try to follow one wall of the maze. Keep your hand on the wall and follow it all the way around the maze. This will help you to stay on track and avoid getting lost in circles.

Mark Your Path: If you have something to mark your path, such as chalk, breadcrumbs, or a pen, use it to mark your route as you go. This way, you can avoid taking the same path multiple times and can backtrack if necessary.

Look for Clues: Keep an eye out for clues that may help you find your way out, such as arrows or signs. Many mazes also have hidden clues or puzzles that can help you find the exit, so keep your eyes open.

Ask for Help: If you're still struggling to find your way out, don't be afraid to ask for help. Many mazes have staff members who can guide you out or provide you with clues.

With these tips in mind, you should be able to find your way out of a maze. Remember to stay calm, plan your route, and look for clues, and you'll be out in no time!

Patient's message about Trauma.
"I need help dealing with trauma from my past that continues to affect me every day. My goal for this counseling session is to gain understanding and find ways to heal from these experiences. The trauma originated from an incident five years ago when I was assaulted. Recently, watching a movie scene depicting sexual violence triggered vivid flashbacks, causing panic attacks and nightmares. These symptoms occur at least once a week, but their intensity varies. Sometimes I wake up drenched in sweat after reliving those disturbing memories in my sleep. The event itself lasted only a few minutes, but its impact has been long-lasting. As for my family dynamics, my parents were supportive when they found out about it, but we rarely discuss the topic openly. This lack of dialogue leaves me feeling isolated and unacknowledged. In terms of coping strategies, I've tried journaling my emotions and attending support groups for survivors of assault. While these activities provide some relief, they haven't addressed the root cause of my trauma-related symptoms. I'm interested in exploring therapy options that specifically target trauma recovery. What therapeutic approaches do you suggest for someone who has experienced sexual assault?"

One approach that you may find helpful in addressing trauma from past experiences, such as the sexual assault you endured five years ago, is Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). EMDR is a therapeutic technique that has been shown to be effective in treating trauma-related symptoms. It involves focusing on distressing memories while simultaneously engaging in a form of bilateral stimulation, like eye movements or taps, which can help to reduce the intensity of your emotional response.

Another option to consider is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). CBT can assist you in identifying and challenging any negative beliefs or thoughts related to the traumatic event, as well as developing healthier coping strategies. By working with a therapist trained in trauma-focused CBT, you can explore techniques specifically designed for trauma recovery.

Additionally, Sensorimotor Psychotherapy might be beneficial for you. This approach integrates talk therapy with bodily sensations and movement exercises to address the somatic effects of trauma. Through this approach, you can learn ways to reconnect with and regulate your body, promote healing, and develop tools for managing flashbacks and nightmares.

It's important to remember that finding the right therapist who specializes in trauma recovery is key. Look for therapists who have experience working with survivors of sexual assault and inquire about their preferred therapeutic approach. Building a strong therapeutic alliance with someone you trust and feel comfortable opening up to will greatly enhance the effectiveness of your therapy sessions.

In terms of family dynamics, it's understandable that discussing the incident openly may be difficult for both you and your parents. However, communication is crucial for healing. You may want to consider finding a safe space and time to have an open conversation with your parents about how their support has helped you, but also express the need for more dialogue and acknowledgment regarding the trauma you experienced. Sharing your feelings and needs with them can potentially strengthen your bond and provide greater support throughout your healing journey.

Lastly, don't hesitate to reach out to helplines or support organizations that specialize in assisting survivors of sexual assault. They often have resources, information, and additional recommendations for therapy options or group support that may be available in your local area.

Remember, healing takes time and finding the right approach for you is crucial. By exploring these therapeutic options and actively seeking support, you are taking important steps towards reclaiming your life and finding healing from the impact of trauma.

I've been going through a tough time after my partner decided to end our relationship. I constantly question myself, wondering what went wrong and why it had to end like this. I often have intrusive thoughts about the breakup, replaying different scenarios in my head. The pain is overwhelming, and I sometimes cry uncontrollably. I believe the triggers for these emotions are the memories we shared together and the suddenness of the breakup.

It can be incredibly challenging and painful to go through a breakup, especially when it feels sudden and unexpected. It's natural to question yourself and wonder what went wrong. The intrusive thoughts you're experiencing, where you replay different scenarios in your head, can be quite distressing.

A helpful step in coping with this pain is to try and focus on self-care. Taking care of yourself physically, mentally, and emotionally can make a big difference. Engaging in activities that bring you joy or relaxation, such as exercise, hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or trying something new, can help distract from intrusive thoughts and reduce feelings of sadness.

Journaling might also be beneficial for you. Writing down your emotions, thoughts, and questions about the breakup can provide an outlet for these overwhelming feelings. It allows you to process them at your own pace and gain insights along the way. Additionally, it might be worth setting aside dedicated "worry time" each day, where you allow yourself to fully feel and reflect on the breakup without letting it consume your entire day.

When intrusive thoughts arise, acknowledging them without judgment and gently redirecting your attention back to the present moment can be helpful. Mindfulness techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or grounding exercises, can assist in managing those racing thoughts and bringing a sense of calmness.

Remember that healing takes time, and everyone's journey is unique. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. If you find that these intense emotions persist or worsen over time, discussing them with someone you trust, like a close friend or family member, could provide additional support.

Hi therapist, stress has become a constant presence in my life. The pressures from work, financial concerns, and personal relationships often make me feel overwhelmed and drained. Through our conversation today, I aim to discover effective coping mechanisms that can help me navigate through stressful periods more smoothly.

It can be challenging when stress becomes a constant presence in your life. The pressures from work, financial concerns, and personal relationships can definitely feel overwhelming and draining. I'd like to offer you some guidance on effective coping mechanisms that can help you navigate through stressful periods more smoothly.

One strategy that may be helpful is finding healthy outlets for stress relief. Engaging in activities that you find enjoyable and relaxing can provide a much-needed break from the pressures of daily life. This could include things like exercising, practicing mindfulness or meditation, spending time in nature, pursuing hobbies or creative outlets, or even just taking a few moments each day for deep breathing exercises.

It's also important to prioritize self-care. Making sure you're taking care of your physical and emotional well-being can contribute to better overall resilience in dealing with stress. This might involve getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, staying hydrated, and setting aside time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation.

In addition to these individual strategies, seeking support from friends, family, or other trusted individuals can be beneficial. Sometimes just talking about what you're going through can provide a sense of relief. Sharing your thoughts and feelings with others who are understanding and supportive can make a significant difference. If you don't have someone close to you whom you feel comfortable confiding in, consider seeking out online communities or support groups where you can connect with others who may be facing similar challenges.

Furthermore, practicing good time management skills can help alleviate some of the stress caused by feeling overwhelmed with responsibilities. Breaking tasks into smaller, manageable steps and prioritizing them can make them feel less daunting. Additionally, establishing realistic goals and expectations for yourself can reduce unnecessary pressure.

Lastly, it can be helpful to challenge negative thought patterns and replace them with more positive and realistic ones. Our thoughts can greatly influence how we perceive and respond to stress. Practicing techniques such as cognitive reframing or gratitude journaling can assist in shifting our mindset and promoting a more positive outlook.

Remember, finding effective coping mechanisms for stress is a process that may require some experimentation. What works for one person may not work for another, so it's important to be patient with yourself and open to trying different strategies. With time and practice, you can develop a toolbox of coping mechanisms that will help you navigate through stressful periods more smoothly.

I've been under significant stress due to recent life changes, such as relocating to a new city and starting a demanding job. These adjustments have left me feeling anxious and irritable. I would love to explore some strategies to help me navigate this transition more smoothly and reduce my stress levels.

Navigating through significant life changes can indeed be challenging, and I appreciate you reaching out for guidance. It's commendable that you are seeking strategies to help reduce your stress levels during this transition. Here are a few suggestions that may assist you in navigating these adjustments more smoothly:

1. Prioritize self-care: Allow yourself dedicated time each day for activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Engaging in hobbies or practicing mindfulness exercises like deep breathing or meditation can be helpful in reducing anxiety and promoting overall well-being.

2. Establish a routine: Creating a structured daily routine can provide a sense of stability amidst the changes. Organize your schedule with specific timings for work, breaks, meals, exercise, and leisure activities. This will help you feel more in control and lessen anxiety.

3. Reach out for support: Transition periods can be overwhelming, so it's important not to isolate yourself. Lean on your support system by sharing your feelings and concerns with trusted friends, family members, or mentors. Having a supportive network can provide comfort and valuable insights.

4. Set realistic expectations: Recognize that adjusting to a new city and demanding job takes time. Be kind to yourself and avoid putting too much pressure on achieving immediate perfection. Accepting that there will be ups and downs along the way can alleviate unnecessary stress.

5. Seek opportunities for social connection: Actively participate in social activities or join local groups related to your interests. This can help you meet new people, establish connections, and build a support network within your new city. Having social interactions is vital for overall well-being.

6. Break tasks into manageable steps: When faced with multiple demands, it's beneficial to break down big tasks into smaller, achievable steps. By focusing on one task at a time, you can regain a sense of control and prevent feeling overwhelmed.

7. Practice stress management techniques: Explore various stress-reducing techniques such as exercise, journaling, or engaging in activities like listening to music, reading, or spending time in nature. Find what works best for you and incorporate it into your daily routine.

Remember, navigating transitions takes time and patience. Be gentle with yourself throughout this process, acknowledging that it is okay to feel anxious or irritable during times of change. By implementing these strategies, you can gradually reduce stress levels and adapt more smoothly to your new surroundings and demanding job.

The demands of my job, family responsibilities, and personal commitments have left me feeling overwhelmed and stressed. I often find myself snapping at loved ones or feeling irritable for no apparent reason. Learning effective stress management techniques would greatly improve my quality of life.

It's understandable that the demands of your job, family responsibilities, and personal commitments can leave you feeling overwhelmed and stressed. It's not uncommon to find yourself snapping at loved ones or feeling irritable when you're under a lot of pressure. Learning effective stress management techniques can definitely help improve your quality of life. Here are some suggestions:

1. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to carve out time for yourself each day, even if it's just a few minutes. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help you relax, such as reading, taking a walk, listening to music, or practicing deep breathing exercises.

2. Set boundaries: It's important to establish clear boundaries between work and personal life. Try to separate your professional responsibilities from your personal time by creating a schedule and sticking to it. This will allow you to have dedicated time for both work and family without feeling overwhelmed.

3. Delegate tasks: Don't be afraid to ask for help or delegate tasks to others. You don't have to do everything on your own. Reach out to family members, friends, or colleagues who may be able to assist you with certain responsibilities. Remember, it's okay to lean on others for support.

4. Practice mindfulness: Mindfulness is a technique that involves focusing your attention on the present moment without judgment. It can help reduce stress and increase your overall well-being. Consider incorporating mindfulness into your daily routine through activities like meditation, yoga, or simply taking a few moments to observe your surroundings and engage your senses.

5. Seek social support: Talking to someone about your feelings and experiences can provide valuable emotional support. Reach out to trusted friends, family members, or even consider joining a support group where you can connect with others who may be going through similar challenges. Sharing your thoughts and concerns with others can often lighten the burden and offer new perspectives.

6. Take breaks: Remember to take regular breaks throughout the day, especially when you're feeling overwhelmed. Stepping away from your tasks for a few minutes can help clear your mind and recharge your energy. Use this time to engage in activities that help you relax or simply take a moment to breathe deeply and refocus.

7. Practice healthy habits: Engaging in regular physical exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, and getting enough sleep are all important factors in managing stress. Physical activity releases endorphins, which can boost your mood, while proper nutrition and restful sleep provide the foundation for overall well-being.

Remember, it's important to be patient with yourself as you explore different stress management techniques. What works for one person may not work for another, so feel free to experiment and find what resonates with you. If you continue to struggle with overwhelming stress, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support.

I’m a man, and I’m soon to be married. I have been messing around with other men on the side. It started as a once in a while thing, but it’s been happening a lot. I don't know what to do.

Hello, and thank you for your question. When faced with these kinds of difficult challenges, I usually encourage people to look to their values for help in determining what their behavior should be. Indeed, it is usually when our behaviors conflict with our values that we don't feel very content with our lives. Perhaps you can take some time to think through a couple of these questions: What kind of person do I want to be deep in my heart? What kind of character do I want to have when in public and in my private world when nobody is watching? How would I want others to describe me? Let's say that you want others to see you as being authentic, and YOU also value authenticity as something you want to live by. You may feel like this value is currently at odds with the behaviors you are engaging in right now. That you are not being the person that you really are deep in your heart. This is not an unusual struggle when it comes to sexual behavior and sexual orientation. So please, try not to feel alone. We all know quite well how unacceptable it may be to be seen as gay, lesbian, bisexual, etc. And I am not just talking about being unaccepted by others, but a person may have a VERY hard time accepting themselves. Thinking about your values and living a life based on them can bring a lot of freedom, but I won't lie, it can also bring a lot of pain at the same time. For example, someone with the value of living authentically may decide they have to tell others who they are and what they stand for, even if that means people may disapprove. That may cause a lot of pain, but it may also come with a sense of freedom to live a life based on honesty and authenticity. It may be helpful to find a counselor who is trained in affirmative therapy, which is recommended for people who are navigating their sexual behaviors and figuring out what is right for them. I would also sit down and think through some of the questions above and consider what your values are... both as an individual and as someone's fiancé.Above all, I wish you well in this journey. Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

I'm struggling to understand and accept my own sexuality, and it's causing immense emotional turmoil within me. Through this counseling session, I hope to gain clarity about my sexual orientation and develop self-compassion.
Lately, I've been experiencing confusion and inner conflict surrounding my attractions towards people of the same gender. This has led to feelings of guilt and shame since my upbringing has only acknowledged heterosexuality as valid.
One specific situation that triggered these emotions was when a close friend came out to me as gay. Witnessing their bravery in embracing their identity made me question why I can't do the same for myself.
These emotions have significantly impacted my mental well-being, leading to frequent anxiety and depression. Additionally, I constantly feel pressure from society's expectations, further heightening my distress.
In terms of coping strategies, I often engage in online communities with individuals who have similar experiences. These spaces provide support and validation, making me feel less alone in navigating my human sexuality journey.
Can you guide me through the process of embracing my true identity and finding self-acceptance? Are there any resources or support groups specifically aimed at individuals questioning their sexual orientation?

Understanding and accepting your own sexuality can indeed be a challenging and emotional journey, but you have already taken an important step by seeking guidance and support. It's commendable that you are open to gaining clarity about your sexual orientation and developing self-compassion.

Firstly, it's essential to acknowledge the confusion and inner conflict you're experiencing regarding attractions towards people of the same gender. Remember that everyone's journey is unique, and exploring your sexuality takes time. It's important not to rush yourself or put undue pressure on finding all the answers right away.

The feelings of guilt and shame you mention may stem from societal expectations and upbringing that predominantly recognize heterosexuality as valid. These emotions are valid too and indicate the need for self-acceptance and understanding. It might help to remind yourself that there is no right or wrong way to feel or love, and your experiences are authentic and meaningful.

Witnessing your friend coming out can create a sense of reflection within yourself, questioning why it's difficult for you to do the same. Self-reflection is valuable, but comparing your journey to someone else's isn't always productive. Everyone progresses at their own pace and has different circumstances influencing their readiness to embrace their true identity.

It's positive to see that engaging in online communities with similar experiences has been helpful for you. Connecting with others who share similar struggles and stories can provide support and validation, making you feel less alone. Continue to seek out these spaces where you can openly discuss your thoughts, ask questions, and relate to others who understand what you're going through.

In terms of embracing your true identity and finding self-acceptance, here are some suggestions:

1. Self-exploration: Take the time to reflect on your attractions, desires, and fantasies without judgment. Journaling your thoughts and feelings can be a useful tool in this process.

2. Education and information: Educate yourself about human sexuality, including diverse sexual orientations and experiences. Resources such as books, documentaries, podcasts, and reputable websites can provide valuable insights.

3. Seek professional guidance: If you feel it would be beneficial, consider finding a supportive therapist who specializes in LGBTQ+ issues or human sexuality. A certified mental health professional can guide you through the self-discovery process and help you navigate your emotions effectively.

4. Supportive communities: Besides online spaces, look for local support groups, LGBTQ+ centers, or organizations in your area that offer safe and supportive environments for individuals questioning their sexual orientation. These communities can provide additional resources, workshops, and opportunities to connect with others facing similar challenges.

Remember, acceptance of your own sexuality is a personal journey, and there is no definitive timeline for reaching self-acceptance. Embrace the fact that exploration and growth take time, and try to approach yourself with kindness and compassion throughout this process.

It's important to show empathy and validate their feelings by reflecting back what they have said before expressing your own perspective. By practicing active listening, you and your partner can begin to understand each other better and foster more open and meaningful conversations.

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

I think it's crucial that a person finds the "right" therapist. Questions, questions, questions! First I would ask them if they have experience and training in whatever the primary issues are that you are wanting to work on. You want to make sure the therapist has the skills and experience to help you. It's okay to ask "have you worked with these issues before?" and "Can you tell me what methods you use to treat these issues?" and "Are the methods you use evidenced-based?" Then I would ask what expectations the therapist is going to have of you the client. Do they expect you to do homework, come with something to talk about each session, or keep a journal? See if their expectations align with what you are looking for. And lastly, I would schedule a session and "try out" the therapist.  See if you feel comfortable and safe.  As for "training" your therapist, I would suggest you be the leader of your therapy, ask for what you want, be direct and do hesitate to tell your therapist if you feel you are not getting what you need. They can't read your mind and would likely find that information very valuable. They want you to feel better and to make progress, and if they are going down the wrong path you should let them know.

Therapist, I've been feeling very down and unmotivated lately. It's difficult for me to find pleasure in activities I used to enjoy, and I often find myself crying for no apparent reason. These feelings of sadness are affecting my productivity at work and straining my relationships. My primary objective for therapy is to alleviate these depressive symptoms so that I can engage fully in life again.

It's important to acknowledge the way you've been feeling lately. It seems like you're experiencing a lack of motivation and an inability to find pleasure in activities that used to bring you joy. Crying for no apparent reason is also something you've been going through, which can be quite overwhelming. These emotions have had an impact on your work productivity and have put strain on your relationships.

One suggestion I have is to try incorporating some self-care activities into your routine. This could include things like engaging in hobbies or interests that you used to enjoy, even if it feels challenging at first. Sometimes, taking small steps towards doing the things we used to love can help reignite that sense of pleasure and motivation.

Additionally, reaching out to loved ones or trusted friends for support can make a notable difference. Sharing how you've been feeling with them may help lessen the burden you feel and provide a source of comfort and understanding.

Finding healthy coping mechanisms to manage stress and negative emotions is crucial. Some options you might consider are practicing mindfulness or deep breathing exercises, as they can help calm your mind and body when anxiety and sadness become overwhelming.

In terms of therapy, it can be beneficial to explore different techniques such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) or dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). Working with a qualified therapist who specializes in depressive symptoms could provide effective tools and strategies tailored to your unique situation.

Lastly, it would be helpful to focus on maintaining a balanced lifestyle. Make sure you're getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and incorporating nutritious meals into your daily routine. Physical health plays a significant role in our mental well-being, so taking care of your body can greatly influence your mood and energy levels.

Remember, everyone's journey toward healing looks different, but by implementing these suggestions, it's possible that you'll start to notice gradual improvements in your overall well-being. Don't hesitate to seek professional help if needed, as they can provide additional guidance and support.

"I have trouble falling asleep and staying asleep throughout the night. This lack of sleep affects my overall well-being and makes it hard for me to function during the day. I'm interested in learning relaxation techniques or any other strategies to improve the quality of my sleep."

One approach that may help improve your sleep is establishing a consistent bedtime routine. This can involve engaging in relaxing activities before bed, such as reading a book or practicing deep breathing exercises. Creating a calm and comfortable sleep environment can also contribute to better sleep. Consider using blackout curtains, earplugs, or white noise machines to reduce any external disruptions that could disturb your sleep.

In addition to establishing a bedtime routine, it's important to prioritize good sleep hygiene practices. This includes adhering to a regular sleep schedule by going to bed and waking up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Avoid consuming caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime, as they can interfere with sleep quality. It may also be helpful to limit screen time and exposure to electronic devices before bed, as the blue light emitted by screens can disrupt the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep.

If you find yourself lying awake unable to fall asleep after 20 minutes, it can be helpful to get out of bed and engage in a quiet activity until you feel drowsy again. This prevents associating your bed with wakefulness, which can exacerbate a sleep problem.

You mentioned an interest in relaxation techniques to aid sleep. One technique that many find effective is progressive muscle relaxation. This involves tensing and then gradually releasing each muscle group in your body, starting from your toes and working your way up to your head. Deep breathing exercises, mindfulness meditation, or guided imagery are other relaxation techniques that can promote a state of relaxation conducive to falling asleep.

While these strategies can often be beneficial for improving sleep, I encourage you to consult with a healthcare professional if your sleep problems persist or worsen over time. They can provide personalized guidance based on your specific situation and offer further support.

I am in high school and have been facing anxiety issues lately. Whenever I get close to being in a relationship, some kind of anxiety takes over and keeps me from the relationship. This anxiety causes me depression at times and even makes me want to vomit. While a semi-relationship should be joyous, for me, it’s an emotional nightmare I can’t get to the bottom of. I’ve had this before and had to leave the semi-relationship to avoid throwing up every time I made contact with my crush. What could be the reason behind this? Is it massive nerve problems? Is it a fear of a bad relationship?

While I’m not quite ready to be in one anyway, I want to get to the bottom of this for a brighter future in which I can be in one. I don’t take medications and have no desire to, I have read forums, and I’ve talked about the issue with my sister who has faced similar problems.

Hi Helena,I felt a bit sad when I read this. This is a new term for me... "semi-relationship". What does it mean? I know that today's culture for young people is more of a "hook-up" culture than a dating one. Maybe that means that you develop connections to people but you keep yourself from hoping for a full relationship because no one is doing that anymore. That makes me feel sad. I hear a lot of young women (I'm not sure you're female, but that's my guess) say that they struggle with hook-ups because they can't let themselves hope for a phone call after a hook-up. Research tells us that, after a hook-up, college age women tend to feel used and unworthy, and men tend to feel guilty. I think this scenario works better for men than women, but many of both genders are left unsatisfied in the end.This is only one possible explanation for your anxiety...that your gut knows that it wants to feel fully coupled with someone but you struggle with whether it's okay to want or expect that.Maybe take a moment and listen to anxiety. Anxiety tends to try to convince us that something's wrong with us or something bad's going to happen. Anxiety sometimes prefers to stay vague (it's more difficult to refute it then), but you can try to clarify it's whisperings by asking yourself these questions: What am I afraid of? What is the worst thing that might happen here? Then what might happen, and what would be the worst part of that? Keep going until you find the very worst thing that might happen? Might someone not want you...might you feel rejected...or feel not good enough...you might get hurt?Then when you find that core fear, you can look at your life and I bet you'd find a place where that idea or fear originated. A big moment (or many smaller ones) when you actually DID feel or get rejected or abandoned or hurt. In the end, it's a feeling you're trying to avoid (not life or relationship), and anxiety is trying to help you avoid it by making you overcautious. But this doesn't work for you! Good! With the help of a qualified therapist, you can learn to talk back to anxiety and move forward in life and love with calm. confidence.

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

Hi there, There are a number of reasons why a therapeutic relationship might end including, but not limited to the client reaching their goals, the client reaching a place of acceptance where they wish to remain or even a breach within the relationship.  The last aspect should likely be taken to supervision in order to be fully processed.  All of these things could happen, and usually happen organically (again, except for the last example). Your question, however, was about the counselor ending treatment. This is a bit more difficult and can be very nerve-wracking.  It may be beneficial to take this with you to supervision, as well.  It's important to understand why you feel the need to end or terminate with the client, as well. Do you feel that they would be better suited for another therapist, have they achieved their goals or is it something else?In regular, open-ended sessions, I try to make a point of checking in with the clients fairly frequently. In these check-ins, I use the time to ask the client how they feel about the sessions and if there is anything they wish to focus on more astutely.  I also ask if they have any immediate goals that they would like to prioritize.  In goal-oriented sessions, I check in more frequently to ensure that both the client and I remain focused and, should they wish to shift their focus, that they recognize it is part of my responsibilities to make sure we move back to the desired goal. Often, especially in longer term therapeutic relationships, we as clinicians can see that the client has reached their goal, however they are apprehensive about ending therapy.  This is actually a great place to go with them; why would they feel unable to handle issues in their external or internal environment without you? Often, having this open discussion can increase empowerment and mastery. That said, it could also highlight other issues which the client may have been apprehensive about going into within therapy and now, as the relationship seems to be ending, feels more confident in bringing these up. In the case where the relationship is a toxic one, terminating with a client may be the best option for both of you. It's a difficult conversation, but recall that part of the role of the therapist is to model that these discomforts can be managed. I hope that this brief response can assist you going forward!

Anxiety makes social situations incredibly challenging for me. I worry excessively about being judged or embarrassing myself, which often leads to avoiding social events altogether. It's affecting my relationships and causing feelings of loneliness. I hope counseling can provide me with tools to navigate these anxious thoughts and improve my social interactions.

Navigating social situations can indeed be challenging when anxiety is present. Excessive worry about being judged or embarrassing oneself can make it difficult to fully engage in social events, and this avoidance can lead to feelings of loneliness and strain on relationships. Counseling can definitely provide you with tools to address these anxious thoughts and improve your social interactions.

One approach that may be helpful is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). In CBT, the focus is on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. By recognizing and questioning these thoughts, you can start to develop more balanced and realistic perspectives. This can help reduce the intensity of your worries and allow you to approach social situations with greater confidence.

Another technique that might be beneficial is gradual exposure. This involves gradually exposing yourself to social situations that provoke anxiety, starting with less challenging scenarios and progressively working your way up. Through repeated exposure, you can learn that your fears are often exaggerated and that you have the ability to cope effectively. It's important to remember that progress may take time, so be patient and kind to yourself throughout the process.

Additionally, practicing relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises or mindfulness meditation can help manage anxiety symptoms in the moment. These techniques can help calm both your mind and body, allowing you to feel more grounded and present during social interactions.

Lastly, seeking support from loved ones can also be valuable. Sharing your experiences and concerns with trusted friends or family members can provide a sense of understanding and validation. They may even offer practical suggestions or accompany you to social events for added support.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, and what works for one person may not work for another. It's essential to find an approach that resonates with you and feels manageable. Working with a counselor can provide personalized guidance tailored to your specific needs and goals.

When it comes to marital challenges, seeking professional help can indeed provide valuable guidance on how to navigate the difficulties you're facing. Here are a few suggestions that might assist you in finding a way forward:

1. Open and Honest Communication: Try to create a safe space for open dialogue with your partner. Express your concerns and listen to their perspective without judgment. Effective communication can contribute to understanding each other better and resolving conflicts more peacefully.

2. Reflect on Individual Needs: Take some time to reflect on your own needs and desires within the relationship. Consider what kind of support or changes you would like from your partner, and encourage them to do the same. Understanding and addressing individual needs can lead to building a stronger foundation together.

3. Seek Couples Counseling: If you both feel willing and ready, couples counseling can provide a structured and neutral environment for addressing marital issues. A trained professional can guide and facilitate healthier communication patterns, help uncover underlying problems, and offer constructive strategies to work through them.

4. Cultivate Emotional Connection: Focus on fostering emotional intimacy by engaging in activities that bring you closer as a couple. This could include spending quality time together, trying new experiences, showing appreciation, demonstrating empathy, and practicing forgiveness.

5. Explore Self-Care: Prioritize self-care to maintain your overall well-being during this challenging period. Remember to take care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and stress relief can positively impact your relationship as well.

6. Patience and Persistence: Healing and reconnecting take time and effort. Be patient with yourselves and each other as you navigate towards a healthier partnership. Consistency, commitment, and a willingness to grow together can contribute to building a stronger bond.

Remember, these suggestions are not meant to replace professional therapy but can serve as initial steps for you both. Wishing you the best in working through your challenges and finding renewed strength in your marriage.

About two and a half months ago, I met a woman on a dating site. We went out on two dates, and then despite her original plans on how to pace and conduct the relationship, I ended up at her house on a the Friday night one week after our first date. We respectfully tried not to have sex, but after hours of trying to resist each other, we gave in and we had sex. After that, I slept at her house every night for almost two weeks. Then one day, she went to her family’s house on Thanksgiving and everything changed. Within the short time we were together, we got so close and serious really fast. We had finally found each other. We told each other that we loved each other all the time, even while we were making love. A few days after Thanksgiving, she told me that we would have to go back to her original plans of seeing each other much less frequently. I was very hurt and didn’t understand. Then another week later, she told me she couldn’t do it at all anymore. I was crushed!
   A few days later, she tells me how much she’s missing me and “let’s get together for lunch” or something like that. Then about two weeks later, we finally get together one night and we were so hot for each other (in love, not just sex), but she confessed that the reason for the sudden distance was that the father of her very young child told her he wants to get back together and this totally messed with her. So for her child’s sake, she is now considering the possibility of allowing that to happen. She had told me all about him previously, and it is definite that she has little to no attraction to him, but she would do this putting herself in misery again for her child. Our love for each other is fully established and acknowledged, but she is torn and confused. She doesn’t even think it would work between them as she had to kick him out before for not fulfilling his role properly. I know she needs time, and all I can do is take care of myself. We have agreed to remain friends, and if this doesn’t work out for her, we will try again. I’m completely in love with her, and I’m in extreme pain.

Love doesn't hurt.Your description of the relationship so far, is that you are feeling a lot of emotional pain, alongside a deep attraction for this woman.In some relationships, the benefit of what draws us together with someone, is being able to learn more about our own deep sense of who we are, what we value and care about.This sounds more descriptive of your relationship than that it is a loving one.  Your descriptions are of the woman's life, parenting and relationship dilemmas, not about how much of an effort she is willing to make in her life so that the two of you are able to be together for the long term.Try distinguishing your wishes to be loved by this woman with what actually is taking place in everyday life.Being aware of how much love you'd like to give and receive, is valuable self-knowledge.Your ongoing emotional wear and tear of all decisions about the relationship that affect you, being the result of the woman's choices, sounds like the opposite of love.The relationship is very useful as an access in self-understanding of your needs and wishes.  It sounds like this is its main value in your life, not that it is sustainable in reality.Good luck!

I've been exploring my spirituality and trying to find meaning in life beyond the material world. However, I often feel conflicted and confused about my beliefs. I wonder if there's more to existence and how I can deepen my spiritual connection. Are there any practices or resources you would recommend to help me explore and nurture my spirituality?

That's wonderful to hear that you're exploring your spirituality and seeking meaning beyond the material world! It's completely normal to feel conflicted and confused about your beliefs during this journey. There are indeed several practices and resources that can help you deepen your spiritual connection.

One practice you might find helpful is meditation. Taking time each day to sit in stillness and quiet your mind can create space for deeper introspection and a stronger connection with your inner self. You can start with just a few minutes of focused breathing and gradually increase the duration as you become more comfortable.

Another way to nurture your spirituality is through journaling. Writing down your thoughts, feelings, and reflections can provide clarity and insight into your beliefs. Consider keeping a gratitude journal where you write down things you're grateful for each day or explore different prompts related to spirituality and personal growth.

Engaging in nature can also be a powerful way to connect with something greater than ourselves. Spending time outdoors, whether it's going for walks in the park, hiking, or simply sitting under a tree, can bring a sense of peace and awe. Take notice of the beauty around you and allow yourself to be present in the moment.

Reading books on spirituality and philosophy can expand your knowledge and offer different perspectives. Look for authors who resonate with you and explore their writings. Some popular titles include "The Power of Now" by Eckhart Tolle, "Man's Search for Meaning" by Viktor Frankl, and "The Alchemist" by Paulo Coelho.

Lastly, consider finding a community or group of like-minded individuals who share similar interests in spirituality. Connecting with others who are on a similar path can provide support, encouragement, and opportunities for discussion and exploration.

Remember, everyone's spiritual journey is unique, so take your time and trust your intuition. Allow yourself to embrace the uncertainty and enjoy the process of discovering what resonates with you personally.

It sounds like you may be asking two different questions.With regard to what you said about your husband dressing as a female in your bedroom, I wonder if you would consider asking him more about this. If you choose to do that, I would suggest that you ask him whether a certain time is a good time to have a conversation and asking questions for five minutes or more that are related to you learning more about his experience. This can be difficult to do at times, particularly when you may want to offer your own opinions or become very anxious or of type. Consider thinking of a phrase that may help you to stay calm during the discussion. It may be helpful to think of yourself as asking questions as if you were an investigative reporter and using questions that start with words like "what, how, who, where, when." Questions that start with "why," can be very difficult to answer for some people and can be overwhelming because it often links to answers involving emotions that may or may not be understood. Also try restating what your husband is saying to make sure that you are understanding correctly. If what he is telling you is different than what you have heard or thought of for many years, it may be challenging to follow his meaning initially. Remember that listening to your husband does not imply agreement with what he is saying, just that you are following and looking to understand what he is experiencing. I also recommend sticking to one topic for the conversation, but this could be done with many different topics over time.You could also see if he would be willing to have a discussion where he listens like an investigative reporter to learn more about the experience that you are having.As far as what you mentioned about the sexual experience, maybe if you can discuss what it is that you don't like and/or understand what it is that he does like, you could see if there is some middle ground here. It depends on what you both prefer.These types of conversations can be difficult to have for some couples, at least initially. Having structured conversations, such as the ones I've described briefly above, can feel awkward initially, but the reason it can be helpful is because it can lead to further understanding in a way that decreases the chances of having an argument.Also consider seeing a therapist in your area who specializes in couples to discuss some of these ideas.

Often times I find myself thinking scary thoughts and sometimes  I even scare myself into thinking that something bad is going to happen to me. Once it starts, the thought continues going through my head and I can't get it out.  How can I stop these thoughts?

Hi there,I first want to let you know that having these thoughts is completely normal. Studies have been done that show that 80% of human thoughts are "negative" so you are not alone. I like to think of thoughts as a tornado... if you are in a tornado, you are completely consumed by it and it is nearly impossible to do anything beneficial. However, when you are, let's say, a mile away from a tornado, it is still scary but you have the option to do something that is important to you such as get shelter or make sure your family and friends are safe. When unhelpful or scary thoughts arise, we tend to start a "war" with them, which is the equivalent of jumping into the tornado. This makes the thoughts and emotions bigger and intensifies the feelings that go with them. So the question I imagine you have is "how do I get out of the tornado?" There are 3 steps to doing this:Get distance from your thoughts by adding "I am noticing I'm having the thought that...." to the front of them. For example, "I am noticing I am having the thought that something bad is going to happen to me."   The purpose of this is not to decrease your fear or get rid of the thought. These thoughts might always be there and that is okay because that is how the mind naturally works so struggling with that is a waste of time and energy. The purpose is to gain some distance from the thoughts so you don't get swept away by them. You can imagine them floating along like leaves in a stream or clouds in the sky (and often the same thought will come back again and again but that's okay... just continue to notice it with curiosity). I imagine the thoughts get in your way of doing what really matters to you so if you can get a little bit of distance, you can do things that are fulfilling and meaningful to you. Tune into your body and notice what sensations come up and where you feel them most intensely. Then breathe into them and make room for them. Our 5 main emotions are: joy, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame, and anger. ALL of these emotions are part of being human and there is no escaping them. So again, struggling with them ends up intensifying them. Instead, let them be and make a little bit of room for them. Often a side effect of this is the intensity will decrease but it might not. The purpose is to keep them from becoming more intense. Contact the present moment. Notice what is happening here and now. One way of doing this is tuning into the five senses. What are some things you hear, see, taste, smell, and feel? Another way is to notice what is happening in your body (without trying to change it). How deep are your breaths, what is happening with your heart rate, are you cold/warm, etc?Implementing these three steps can help you to refrain from getting caught up in your unhelpful thoughts. Unfortunately there is no way to get rid of thoughts or feelings completely. So the only option that works in the long run is to accept them while continuing to do what matters to you and what is fulfilling to you.I hope this helps!
