Is there anything that's specifically causing the stress? Probably some big changes?
My job safety, financial situation, get evicted and much more.
It sounds like you're facing some potential instability which can definitely increase anxiety. What strategies have you been trying so far?
None so far. I have no idea. Any suggestions?
For the short term, have you tried looking in to meditation or breathing exercises? For a longer approach, have you thought about gaining some new skills for the job market?
Oh ok. That is helpful. I've been reading to past the time.
Sounds like reading might be a good way to get your mind out of the anxiety loop, does that sound right?
Yes, sometimes.
That's great! Maybe you can take that a step further and read some material on mindfulness
Not my type of books, but I'll definitely look into it. Job stability is also a concern for me I definitely fear for my future if I lose my job.
So, you don't feel like you have a secure spot right now, is that right?
That is correct.
Can you tell me what your job is?
I work for an insurance company. Low level employee.
Ok, have there been any talks about layoffs? Or any concerns about your performance?
No, but due to this pandemic, layoff is a concern.
So you're nervous about things that might happen in the future, but there's no talks about anything concrete?
I am feeling really down.
I'm sorry to hear you're feeling that way, what has you feeling this way?
My husband and I have 4 kids. One of those children is a child from his previous marriage. We constantly argue about how he favors that child over our other 3.
Oh no, that's not good. Do the other kids see it as well?
2 of the children are younger so they do not realize it but the other child is older and definitely notices.
Does your husband realize that the other child notices it and how it hurts them?
I have told him but he is in denial of the whole situation.
Why do you think he favors that child? Is that child only with you part-time that he feels he needs to make the most of that time?

The child is with us every other week and maybe that is why he treats him differently but my husband knows that it is causing problems in our relationship and refuses to change those behaviors. I just do not know what to do anymore.

I understand the frustration, it's hard to see your kids hurting or feeling like they're not enough. Is this the biggest issue you guys are dealing with in your marriage? Or is it just another thing you're not getting along on?
That is very true. This is our main issue. I suppose I need to find someone who is close to us both but not necessarily a family member.
Someone who has seen you interacting as a family and maybe has noticed it as well.
Yes, that is a good idea. Thank you for all of your help. It makes me feel a little better just telling someone about the issue.
Sometimes just getting it off of your chest is all you need to reset. I'm glad that helped and I wish you luck in finding a solution.

I have lately been having lots of anxiety and self-loathing about the fact that I am a young adult virgin girl who has never had a boyfriend before. It seems like everyone my age has already had boyfriends by now or are not virgins anymore, and I just had my first kiss five months ago. I’m worried that, at this rate, I won’t have a boyfriend for a very long time. The problem is that I want to lose my virginity to my first boyfriend who cares about me, but at the same time, I don't want to be waiting forever in order to experience sex. I have already given in to bad temptations by hooking up with random strangers on social media sites and having oral sex with them. Luckily, they were nice guys, but none of them wanted a relationship with me. I feel dirty by doing this, but I feel pressured to do this things in order to seem normal.
   Most people are surprised when they find out that I am a virgin or never had a boyfriend because people think I am really good looking. I am tall, I play lots of sports, and I get excellent grades in school. I am in my first year of university right now, and no guys have approached me to go out on a date or showed any interest. It bothers me. Most of the people in my family have been in relationships at my age already. I feel like I will be single forever sometimes.

I think one of the first questions that springs to mind for me is, "what's the rush?"  Just because other people in your circle have had experiences that you are still warming up to does not mean that there's something wrong or something to be ashamed of.  If anything, I want to commend you on the self-respect you have in wanting to wait and share this most intimate of experiences with someone that will feel the same way about it.  One of the most common distortions in our thinking is when we try to directly compare ourselves to others; while these people and even those in your family share a level of closeness to you they are not exactly like you - they don't see or feel things in the exact same way as you nor do they share the exact same perspective. It's important to be making choices for you and for your own desires and life goals.  Once you stop comparing your happiness, you may find that you are already experiencing it and allow more of your guard to fall down.

I've noticed that whenever I have to make important decisions, I become paralyzed by anxiety. Even simple choices like what to wear or where to eat can trigger intense feelings of panic. I'd like to explore why decision-making is so challenging for me and develop strategies to overcome it.

It can be incredibly overwhelming when anxiety takes over during decision-making moments. The good news is that there are strategies you can try to help overcome this challenge. Here are a few suggestions:

1. Start by identifying the root cause: Take some time to reflect on why decision-making triggers such intense feelings of panic for you. Are there any past experiences or underlying fears that might be contributing to this? Understanding the source of your anxiety can provide valuable insights into how to address it.

2. Break decisions down into smaller steps: Sometimes, the weight of making important choices can feel paralyzing. To make it more manageable, try breaking down the decision into smaller, more digestible steps. Focus on one aspect at a time and give yourself permission to take things gradually.

3. Gather information and explore options: Decision-making becomes easier when you have all the necessary information at hand. Take the time to gather relevant facts and explore different options before making a choice. This process can help alleviate anxiety by providing a sense of control and clarity.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Anxiety often feeds on negative thoughts and worst-case scenarios. When faced with decision-making anxiety, try to identify any irrational or unhelpful thoughts that may be fueling your panic. Then, consciously challenge those thoughts by considering alternative perspectives or evidence that contradicts them.

5. Practice self-care and relaxation techniques: Taking care of your overall well-being can significantly impact your ability to manage anxiety during decision-making. Engage in activities that promote relaxation, such as deep breathing exercises, mindfulness meditation, or physical exercise. Prioritizing self-care can help reduce overall anxiety levels and increase resilience.

6. Seek support from trusted individuals: Don't hesitate to reach out to supportive friends, family members, or mentors who can offer guidance and reassurance during decision-making processes. Sharing your concerns with someone you trust can provide an outside perspective and help ease the burden of anxiety.

Remember, overcoming decision-making anxiety takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself as you explore these strategies and find what works best for you. If your anxiety persists or becomes unmanageable, consider seeking professional help from a mental health expert who can provide personalized guidance tailored to your specific needs.

My boyfriend won't touch me intimately, he won't kiss me while we are having sex and he won't have oral sex with me. I know he has done this things with other women in the past. I don't know why he won't do them with me. What should I do?

First off, don't blame yourself or be too quick to jump to any scary conclusions.  Human sexuality can be incredibly complex at times (e.g., what turns us on at one time may not be what turns us on the next time). There could actually be a number of things going on including him having performance anxiety...maybe he had a bad experience with a previous partner that's left him scared to try again (we call this operant conditioning).  It could also be that he puts you in a different category than previous lovers.  Sometimes I refer to this as the "hooker-housewife mentality" where a partner somehow gets the idea that when we truly fall in love, we treat that one differently; almost up on a pedestal.  Drives many partners crazy until they're aware that this is going on and give their boyfriend/ girlfriend permission to enjoy both the naughty and the nice with them. It could also be that he's not even aware that he's not doing these things. If you haven't asked him yet, you might try gently approaching the subject when you're not already in the bedroom or trying to get in on and inquire what he most enjoys about sex with you (or has enjoyed in the past, or thinks he might enjoy).  You can also share your favorite highlights of sex with him.  Give him an ego boost and tell him what he does well while then asking him if he'd be down to go downtown.  "Baby, it REALLY turns me on when you kiss me during sex."If you continue to get the impression that it's somehow only about YOU or that he's just really hesitant to talk about sex in general, you might see if he'd be cool to chat with a counselor who specializes in sexual intimacy.

Something happened this summer that I cannot forgive myself for. When I think about what happened, I feel ashamed and guilty even though my loved ones forgave me.

Hi Ohio, I totally get how it can be more difficult to forgive ourselves than to forgive others. My guess is that you tend to come down too hard on yourself a lot. That's a huge barrier to happiness that you can work to reduce. I'll get you started.You feel shame in a debilitating way that is probably way out of proportion to the incident. Is it triggering some old shame? Unfortunately, a lot of adults use shame as a motivator for kids. It doesn't work. When was the first time you remember feeling a lot of shame, as in "I'm bad", or "I'm worthless"? Is there a younger version of you who is still feeling shame over something that wasn't your fault? Sometimes shame shadows are connected to an absent or hurtful parent, sexual abuse or some family loss or trauma. If so, picture yourself at that age. Can you tell your child self that whatever horrible thing happened to them isn't their fault? Can you have compassion for that child who first felt shame or had shame heaped on them? That's your first goal...to go to the source of the shame and heal that child's wound with compassion. What happens to children is never their fault (and fault is a pretty useless concept anyway).Once you take the layers of old "I'm bad" shame off, the load is lighter and you can use self talk to further reduce the shame. Here are some things you can say to yourself...every day...I'm human and that's okay. I don't have to be perfect.I can have compassion for my mistakes.I can feel proud that I'm facing my mistake and making things right.I deserve forgiveness and compassion, and I have that for other people too.There's no purpose to holding on to shame.I can learn from my mistakes and move forward.Everyone makes mistakes.Other people don't want me to carry this shame around.I don't need shame to remind me not to do it again. I've figured that out.Shame tries to convince you that you need to carry "it" around in order to prevent further mistakes. Poppycock.  You've learned your lesson, now you can move forward to other mistakes. Sorry...but you're human and you'll keeping making... hopefully different, glorious mistakes. Embrace the learning. Lean into the experiences of life. It's all juicy stuff, and you're in good company; we're all in the same position of being mortal.

It's understandable that you feel disconnected and struggle to form meaningful relationships given your experiences. It's important to acknowledge that feelings of isolation and disconnection are common, especially in today's fast-paced world. However, it's also crucial to recognize that these feelings can stem from various sources, including past experiences, current situations, and even our own thought patterns.

Your experience at the party is a clear example of social anxiety, which can be a significant barrier to forming connections. Social anxiety is a common mental health condition characterized by fear, discomfort, and avoidance of social situations due to feelings of embarrassment, self-consciousness, and perceived judgment from others. This fear can manifest in various ways, such as difficulty making eye contact, speaking up in groups, or even attending social events.

To help you overcome this challenge, we can explore various therapeutic approaches. One effective method is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on changing negative thought patterns and behaviors. We can work together to identify and challenge the thoughts and beliefs that contribute to your social anxiety, such as the belief that you must always be perfect or that others are judging you. We can also practice various techniques, such as relaxation exercises, role-playing, and exposure therapy, to help you build confidence and improve your social skills.

Another approach that may be helpful is mindfulness-based interventions, which can help you become more aware of your thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations in the present moment. By learning to accept and observe these experiences without judgment, you can reduce the emotional intensity of social situations and improve your ability to connect with others.

Ultimately, the goal of our therapeutic sessions will be to help you develop a deeper understanding of your social anxiety and the ways it manifests in your life. Through a collaborative and compassionate approach, we can work together to identify the root causes of your feelings of isolation and disconnection and develop effective strategies for overcoming them. This process will involve a commitment to self-reflection, open communication, and a willingness to explore new ways of thinking and behaving.

As we embark on this therapeutic journey, I want to assure you that you are not alone in your struggles. I am here to support you, to listen, and to help you find the tools and resources you need to build stronger, more meaningful relationships. Together, we can work to challenge your social anxiety and help you connect with the world around you.

It's important to acknowledge that these experiences can contribute to heightened levels of anxiety. While I'm not a mental health expert, there are some general strategies that individuals often find helpful in managing anxiety.

One approach that could be beneficial is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and challenging negative thoughts and beliefs that contribute to anxiety. Through CBT, you might explore any unhelpful thinking patterns or fears related to judgment and work towards developing more balanced perspectives. Additionally, therapists who specialize in trauma-focused therapies may also be able to help you process and heal from your previous traumatic event.

In addition to therapy, self-care practices play an essential role in managing anxiety. You mentioned trying deep breathing exercises and mindfulness meditation, which are excellent techniques. However, it's worth noting that different practices resonate with different individuals, so exploring several options might be beneficial. Some people find journaling their thoughts, engaging in regular physical activity, practicing relaxation exercises such as progressive muscle relaxation, or connecting with supportive friends or loved ones helpful in managing anxiety.

As everyone's individual experiences differ, what works for one person may not work for another. Remember to approach this process with patience, as finding the right tools may involve some exploration.

That is a really tough situation that a lot of young people are experiencing right now. The first thing to under is that you can’t change who your parents are and cannot change their behavior. The thing to keep in mind is that you can control your responses and actions.  You may need to keep living at home with them for the next few months or years and the best way to do this is to have a plan. The second thing is to keep in mind that their controlling behavior is most likely not about based your behavior. Controlling parents are often driven by their concept of what will keep their children safe and happy. Unfortunately this is not always accurate but keep in mind it is not a personal attack.  There are ways you can deal with controlling parents – and most of them require creating a plan of action.Examples of action plans:Decide in advance how you’ll calmly and rationally respond to your parents when you feel they’re trying to control youArrange to phone a friend or trusted adult when you feel like you’re losing controlTalk in person to an adult you trust. There aren’t any quick tips on how to deal with parents who want to control you; you need to find strategies that are geared to your specific family situation. Get specific coping tips from books about family dynamics, such as:Toxic Parents: Overcoming Their Hurtful Legacy and Reclaiming Your Life by Susan ForwardCutting Loose: An Adult's Guide to Coming to Terms with Your Parents by Howard HalpernA counselor can be a good resource and provide support and guidance about issues addressing normal growth and development during periods of transition.

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

Hello and thanks for your question! It's important to have the right therapist. I encourage you to start by checking out the website of the therapist. Their blog articles will reflect the kind of work they do and the approach they may take while working with you. If there's an email listed, go ahead and reach out. Ask the particular questions that are on your mind. Share a little of what you are looking for in a therapist. Are you a goal-direct, solution-focused individual who is looking for someone to listen and ask questions? Are you less self-directive and desire a therapist who can give you the consistent push to move forward? Are you interested in intertwining certain theory approaches? Maybe a cognitive-base or experiential? Art therapy or engaging in exercise while talking? Your therapist is out there. It's OK to try out a therapist for a session or two. Interview them as they interview you. It's also OK to change therapists; ask your present therapist for a referral. He or she should be willing to provide you with names of other providers and there's no shame in asking for it. You deserve to work with someone who fits your style!I imagine there's already enough things happening in your life if you are searching for a therapist. Do you really want to "train" your therapist? After all, you are paying them for their knowledge and expertise. It does take time to develop a relationship and developing one with your therapist is vital to your growth and satisfaction. Participating in therapy, for the most part, should be a time you anticipate and not avoid. Can you be honest with them? Are you trusting of the confidentiality they provide? Has this person clearly shared with you the limits of confidentiality if using insurance versus paying privately? Is there any part of you that "just isn't sure"? It's okay to assert yourself in therapy. As a therapist, I invite you to assert yourself as it's a way to develop self-confidence and resiliency. Not everyone thrives in therapy by sitting in an office or lounging on a couch. Some folks benefit by challenging themselves in various environments, or are more comfortable in their homes, online, in the community, at a retreat, etc. Give yourself a gift of spending some time finding the person that can work with you towards what you are searching. Although there's the convenience of the local non-profit agency in your area, it may not be what you need. Also, limiting yourself to the names of providers listed on your insurance may not lead to the "right one". There are many forms of therapy that insurances refuse to cover. When this happens, many times you can be reimbursed for your expenses by your insurance or you can use a Health Savings Card or Flexible Spending Card, there are many, many options. Therapy is about exploring yourself. Go ahead and feel free!If you feel as if you need to "train" your therapist, it seems that person is not the right fit for you. Engaging in treatment should be quite comfortable from the outset of treatment. Many independent practitioners or small group providers offer a free consultation to start the relationship. Perhaps that's a place for you to begin? Good luck and I wish you well!

I've recently developed a fear of traveling by plane. Even though I used to enjoy flying, now the idea of being in an enclosed space for hours triggers intense anxiety and panic. It's preventing me from visiting family and going on vacations. I want to explore the underlying reasons behind this fear and work towards overcoming it.

It's understandable that your fear of traveling by plane is causing you distress and limiting your ability to visit family and go on vacations. It's great that you want to explore the underlying reasons behind this fear and work towards overcoming it. Here are some suggestions and guidance for you:

1. Educate yourself about flying: Understanding how planes work, safety measures, and statistics can help alleviate some of your fears. Look for information from reliable sources or even consider reading books or watching documentaries about air travel.

2. Gradual exposure: Start small and gradually expose yourself to situations related to flying. For example, you can start by visiting an airport and observing planes take off and land. Then, try taking short flights before gradually increasing the duration. This step-by-step approach can help build confidence over time.

3. Relaxation techniques: Practicing relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness can help manage anxiety symptoms during flights. These techniques can be learned through self-help resources like books, apps, or online videos.

4. Cognitive-behavioral strategies: Challenge and reframe any negative thoughts or beliefs related to flying. Identify and replace irrational thoughts with more realistic ones. For instance, remind yourself of the statistically low chances of accidents or focus on positive aspects of air travel, such as reaching your destination quickly.

5. Seek support from a trusted companion: Consider traveling with someone who understands your fear and provides emotional support. Having a familiar and supportive person by your side can make the experience less overwhelming.

6. Find distractions: Engage in activities during the flight that distract your mind from anxious thoughts. Bring a book, listen to music, watch movies, or do puzzles. Keeping your mind occupied can help reduce anxiety levels.

7. Professional counseling support: If your fear persists or becomes too difficult to manage on your own, seeking assistance from a mental health professional specializing in anxiety disorders may be beneficial. They can provide personalized strategies and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, overcoming fears takes time and patience. Celebrate small victories along the way and be kind to yourself throughout the process. Good luck on your journey towards overcoming your fear of flying!

Hello
How are you?
I've gone to a couple therapy sessions so far and still everytime I walk in I get nervous and shaky. Is this normal? Should I still be feeling like this?

Hello. First, I am so sorry you are experiencing these feelings. They can be intense, I will do my best to offer some suggestions or thoughts that I hope will be helpful to you. There could be a number of things occurring. Therapy is a delicate, private decision and I would first like to commend you for the fact that you are not giving up, that you are working to figure this out, and make this work, it sounds like you are engaged and motivated to receive support from a professional, your continued  dedication and motivation will take you far. I would first start by asking if you have discussed this with your therapist, if you feel comfortable enough telling your therapist what is going on, maybe inform the therapist that  that you feel nervous and shaky. I am a firm believer in open communication between the client and therapist as this builds a healthy therapeutic relationship that yields positive outcomes, if this can be obtained and well received. This is YOUR time for healing and therapy should be a safe, supportive environment to not only process but to seek support and guidance from a professional who can help you move past the barriers. Remind yourself what you are working to achieve, close your eyes in a safe moment and breathe in and out slowly, in slowly through your nose and out through your mouth with pursed lips. I know it may sound kind of silly but they really work and are incredibly helpful. We often forget to breathe, especially when we  are feeling anxious. You are supported here and try taking yourself through the above thought process and breathing and practice the breathing several times a day. I hope this shaky and uneasy feeling eases. Wishing you the very best!Laura Cassity, LMSW, LMAC

What do I do if I have been feeling like I could never be with anyone because no one would want me. Or I couldn't have many friends because of who I am. It's strange I want to be loved but I'd hate to be because I always lose.

As a relationship therapist I work with a lot of people who feel similar feelings to some degree or another and almost always find that the origin of these feelings point back towards childhood. How did you caregivers express (or not express) love towards you? How did they express (or not express) love towards one another. These early messages become your template for how you have learned to see yourself and what you expect from others. In his book Wired for Love, Stan Tatkin, PsyD writes “We learn to love ourselves precisely because we have experienced being loved by someone. We learn to take care of ourselves because somebody has taken care of us. Our self worth and self-esteem also develop because of other people.”  This could be very fruitful to explore in individual therapy with a relationship therapist who really gets it, you may have to interview a few to find the right fit; that's OK. Maybe you'd even want to read that book I linked above. :) Noticing this pattern is HUGE, it's where transformation begins. And now that you have be kind with yourself, it begins there too.

Lately, I've noticed that I struggle to connect with others on a deeper level. While I have acquaintances and casual friendships, I long for more meaningful connections. It seems like I have difficulty opening up and expressing my true thoughts and feelings. This leaves me feeling disconnected and misunderstood. I wonder if there are any strategies or techniques that could help me foster stronger social relationships and create lasting bonds with others.

I can understand how frustrating it must be to feel like you're struggling to connect with others on a deeper level. It's completely normal to long for more meaningful connections and to want to express your true thoughts and feelings. Building stronger social relationships takes time and effort, but there are definitely strategies that can help.

One technique you could try is actively listening to others when they speak. Instead of focusing on what you'll say next, really pay attention to what the other person is saying. Show genuine interest by asking follow-up questions and reflecting back on what they've shared. This can create a sense of trust and understanding in your conversations.

Another strategy is to practice vulnerability. Opening up and sharing your true thoughts and feelings can be scary, but it can also lead to deeper connections. Start small by gradually expressing yourself more honestly with people you feel comfortable with. As you build trust and see positive reactions, it may become easier to open up further.

Additionally, finding common interests or activities can help foster stronger bonds. Joining clubs, groups, or communities centered around something you enjoy can provide opportunities to meet like-minded individuals who share your passions. Engaging in shared experiences can often lead to deeper connections and lasting friendships.

Remember, building meaningful connections takes time and patience. Be kind to yourself throughout this process and don't put too much pressure on yourself. Keep trying different techniques, and eventually, you'll find the right balance that works for you.

It can be tricky to figure out if a child is truly satisfied with his lack of friendships. Parents can usually tell when their child is happy. But kids who are unhappy may be masking disappointment, perhaps acting out their feelings in an aggressive manner. Others may internalize symptoms, appearing sad or withdrawn. A parent may learn a great deal by asking the teachers questions such as whether the child works with others on group projects or if he eats lunch alone. A parent can also talk with the recess supervisor about what happens on the playground, and whether your child stays on the sidelines of play, unsure of how to join the group. Therespectfully is a difference between kids who are shy but happy and kids who feel isolated because they do not know how to make friends. Itis not necessarily that there is something wrong with that child, but they will in fact need help and suggestions for breaking into a peer group Ask a child if there is someone he would like to have over to play. If a mom or dad can make the play dates happen, or if they hit on an activity the child truly enjoys, the young person may begin to forge friendships on their own. I encourage well-meaning parents to choose words carefully. Use phrases like, "Hey, I noticed something," or "Let me help you be successful." By showing respect, parents should feel more comfortable nudging their children beyond their comfort zone.When to seek professional help. When does isolation raise a red flag for long-term issues? True personality disorders are not typically diagnosed until adulthood. Still, professional counseling should be considered if the anti-social behavior is causing the child significant distress, perhaps keeping him from functioning in everyday activities. Also, parents should pay attention to how the child's social behavior changes over time such as social anxiety. The vast majority of children who define "quality time" as time alone are perfectly happy, healthy and normal. If the child is able to nurture at least one friendship, exhibiting what experts call "social reciprocity," then parents can relax, and can cherish that child who enjoys the pleasure of his or her own company.

Stress has become overwhelming due to recent changes in my personal life and career. In therapy, I would like to identify healthy coping mechanisms to manage these stressors effectively.
For the past few months, things have felt completely chaotic. I ended a long-term relationship, moved to a new city for a job opportunity, and started living alone for the first time. The combination of these significant transitions has left me feeling constantly overwhelmed and emotionally drained. There are nights when I lie awake, replaying conflicts from the past and worrying about the uncertainties of the future. I want to regain control over my life, reduce this overwhelming stress, and find stability amidst all the changes.

To start, it's great that you're seeking therapy to help manage the overwhelming stress that recent changes in your personal life and career have brought about. It sounds like you've gone through a lot of significant transitions in a short period, such as ending a long-term relationship, moving to a new city for a job opportunity, and adjusting to living alone for the first time.

Given these circumstances, it's completely understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed and emotionally drained. Coping with so many changes can be challenging, and it's normal to experience anxiety and uncertainty during this time. 

To regain control over your life and reduce the overwhelming stress, here are some suggestions:

1. Establish a Routine: Create a consistent daily routine that incorporates activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Having a structured schedule can provide stability and help you feel more grounded amidst all the changes.

2. Practice Self-Care: Prioritize self-care activities that promote physical and emotional well-being. This could include engaging in regular exercise, getting sufficient sleep, eating nutritious meals, and setting aside time for hobbies or activities that you enjoy.

3. Reach Out for Support: Don't hesitate to lean on friends, family, or loved ones for support during this time. Sharing your feelings and experiences with trusted individuals can provide comfort and a sense of connection.

4. Set Boundaries: While adapting to new circumstances, it's important to establish healthy boundaries to protect your mental and emotional well-being. Recognize when you need time alone and communicate your needs to others effectively.

5. Mindfulness Techniques: Explore mindfulness techniques, such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or journaling. These practices can help calm your mind, enhance your present-moment awareness, and reduce rumination about past conflicts or future uncertainties.

6. Seek Professional Therapy: Consider finding a therapist who can work with you to develop personalized coping mechanisms and strategies to manage stress. A trained professional can offer guidance and support in navigating these challenging transitions.

Remember, it's essential to be patient with yourself during this process. Change takes time, and it's normal to have ups and downs along the way. By implementing some of these suggestions and working with a therapist, you can regain stability and find ways to effectively manage your stressors.

I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it.    How should I deal with this?

I can only imagine how hard that must have been to hear. On one hand, most of us would say we want our partners to always be honest with us, but on the other disclosures like this can lead to feelings of worry and inadequacy if we're not careful. So let me first of all say that it is very normal for human beings, even very committed and happy partners to have moments where they notice an attraction for someone else. Quite honestly, the brain can't help it. It sees something good looking and it pays attention. And when we pay attention to something good, our brains send out neurochemicals associated with that happy thought...and we get a rush of what your girlfriend is labeling "a crush." The difficulty here is deciphering whether she was just attempting to honor her commitment to you by sharing this feeling OR if she is continuing to feed those feelings. I would encourage you to thank her for being honest if you haven't already, and ask her to further describe the nature of these feelings and what she'd like to do from here. As weird as it is to say, at the end of the day, what helps the most is typically reassuring yourself that you WILL be okay not matter what! That it is worth it to invest in your relationship and give it your all and if someday, god forbid, this woman chooses to walk away, then she is not the one. Will it hurt? Of course. But is it the end? Hell no! There are 7.5 billion people on the planet and I firmly believe statistically speaking alone, there are at least several hundred thousand that could be AMAZING partners for you. Cheering you on,Tamara Powell, LMHCP.S. You might enjoy this excellent book by Esther Perel for further inquiry into the fascinating world of love and mating behaviors: "Mating in Captivity”

Work-related stress has been overwhelming lately. The demands and expectations keep piling up, leaving me feeling burnt out and exhausted. It's challenging to find a healthy work-life balance when the workload seems never-ending. I'd appreciate guidance on setting boundaries, managing time effectively, and finding ways to prioritize self-care amidst a demanding career.

It can be tough when work-related stress starts to take a toll on your well-being. It sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed and exhausted due to the constant demands and expectations at work. Finding a healthy work-life balance can indeed be challenging, especially when it feels like the workload is never-ending.

Setting boundaries is an important step in managing work-related stress. Start by clearly defining your working hours and sticking to them as much as possible. Communicate these boundaries with your colleagues and supervisors so they understand when you are available and when you need time for yourself. Additionally, consider setting limits on how much work you take home or how often you check emails outside of work hours. This will help create a clear separation between work and personal life.

Managing time effectively can also alleviate some of the stress. Prioritize tasks based on their importance and deadlines. Break down larger projects into smaller, more manageable tasks to avoid feeling overwhelmed. Consider using productivity techniques such as the Pomodoro Technique, where you work in focused bursts followed by short breaks, to maintain focus and prevent burnout. Experiment with different strategies to find what works best for you.

Prioritizing self-care is crucial in maintaining overall well-being. Make sure to schedule regular breaks throughout the day to recharge and relax. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help you unwind, whether it's exercising, practicing mindfulness, reading, or spending time with loved ones. Remember that taking care of yourself is not selfish but necessary for your mental and emotional health.

Lastly, don't hesitate to seek support from trusted friends, family members, or even online communities who may have experienced similar challenges. Sharing your feelings and experiences can provide validation and helpful insights. If needed, consider reaching out to a professional therapist who can offer guidance tailored to your specific situation.

Remember, finding a healthy work-life balance takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself as you navigate through this process and remember that you deserve to prioritize your well-being.

1. Start by identifying the specific behaviors that you feel are negatively impacting your life. This could be anything from procrastination or excessive screen time to unhealthy coping mechanisms.

6. Practice self-care regularly. Take time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation. This could include reading, spending time in nature, practicing mindfulness, or engaging in creative outlets.

7. Challenge negative thoughts and beliefs that may be contributing to your current mindset. Replace them with positive affirmations and focus on your strengths and accomplishments.

8. Consider seeking inspiration and guidance from books, podcasts, or online resources that promote personal development and positive thinking.

Remember, change takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself and celebrate even the smallest progress. If you ever feel overwhelmed or stuck, don't hesitate to reach out to your support system for assistance. You're capable of making these positive changes and improving your overall well-being.

One significant contributor to your stress is your overwhelming work responsibilities. Long hours, tight deadlines, and high-pressure situations can certainly create a breeding ground for anxiety. The example you provided of juggling multiple tasks while worrying about meeting expectations is a common experience many people face. To address this, time management skills could be incredibly helpful, allowing you to prioritize tasks and break them down into manageable steps. This approach may alleviate some of the pressure and help prevent feelings of being overwhelmed.

Considering the physical symptoms you mentioned, incorporating regular exercise into your routine may prove beneficial. Exercise has been shown to reduce stress by releasing endorphins and improving overall mood. Additionally, taking short breaks during the day to stretch or practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises could offer relief from tension headaches and muscle soreness.

The family dynamics you described have also played a role in your response to stress. Growing up under constant pressure to excel academically has instilled in you a perfectionist mindset, fear of failure, and an ongoing need for approval. These negative self-beliefs can intensify stress levels and make setbacks feel even more overwhelming. It might be helpful to challenge these thoughts and develop a more realistic perspective on success and personal expectations. Self-compassion exercises, where you treat yourself with kindness and understanding instead of self-criticism, could assist in shifting this mindset and reducing stress.

It's encouraging that you've already tried meditation and breathing exercises. While they didn't provide lasting relief, it's important to note that managing stress is often a combination of various techniques that work together. It may be worth exploring other mindfulness practices, such as grounding exercises or guided imagery, to see if they resonate with you and provide a different level of support.

In counseling, therapists often encourage clients to explore their thoughts and feelings through journaling. Expressing your emotions on paper can be a powerful way to gain insights into patterns or triggers that contribute to stress. Writing could also offer a sense of release and serve as a form of self-reflection.

Lastly, maintaining a healthy lifestyle is crucial for managing stress. This includes ensuring you're getting enough sleep, eating balanced meals, and engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation outside of work. Taking breaks and setting boundaries between work and personal life will help create a better balance and prevent stress overload from continuing to disrupt your well-being.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, and it may take time to find the strategies and tools that work best for you. I hope these suggestions give you some ideas to explore and incorporate into your daily routine as you work towards achieving your goal of regaining balance in your life and effectively managing stress.

Anxiety seems to seep into every aspect of my day. I constantly worry about trivial things, like whether I've made a mistake or offended someone unknowingly. This uneasiness follows me everywhere, making it difficult to relax or be present in the moment. Through counseling, I hope to learn coping strategies to stop my mind from spiraling into anxious thoughts.

It can be challenging to deal with anxiety that impacts every aspect of your day. It's great that you're recognizing how it affects your ability to relax and be present in the moment, as self-awareness is an important first step. Here are some coping strategies that may help you manage anxious thoughts:

1. Practice deep breathing: Taking slow, deep breaths can activate your body's relaxation response and help calm your mind during moments of anxiety. You can try inhaling deeply through your nose for a count of four, holding your breath briefly, and then exhaling slowly through your mouth.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: When you catch yourself worrying or having anxious thoughts, question their validity. Ask yourself if there is concrete evidence supporting these thoughts, and consider more balanced perspectives. Remind yourself that everyone makes mistakes and unintentionally offends others from time to time, but it doesn't mean you're a bad person.

3. Engage in physical activity: Regular exercise has numerous benefits, including reducing stress and anxiety levels. Find activities that you enjoy, whether it's going for walks, practicing yoga, dancing, or playing sports. Physical movement can help distract your mind from anxious thoughts and release endorphins that boost your mood.

4. Establish a daily routine: Having a structured schedule can provide a sense of stability and control, which can be helpful when dealing with anxiety. Try to set aside dedicated times for work/study, leisure activities, self-care, and relaxation. This way, you can better manage your time and prioritize tasks, reducing potential triggers for anxious thoughts.

5. Practice mindfulness: Mindfulness involves intentionally focusing on the present moment without judgment. By training your attention to the here-and-now, you can gradually cultivate a greater sense of peace and reduce anxiety. Start by allocating a few minutes each day for mindful activities such as meditation, deep breathing exercises, or simply paying close attention to your senses and surroundings.

Remember, coping strategies may vary in effectiveness for each individual, and it can take time to find what works best for you. It's also essential to be patient and compassionate with yourself during this process. Seeking support from loved ones or trusted friends could provide additional resources and encouragement along the way.

I have been having a lot of nightmares where I am being killed in different ways. I either wake up in a panic or just crying and sweating. It has made me terrified of falling asleep and is now affecting my daily life too. Can I make the nightmares stop?

Hello, and thank you for your question. Sleep problems, including insomnia and even the nightmares that you are writing about, are really common for people and so many people suffer from them. Here are a few things to consider or to try: 1. Have you changed or started taking any new medication lately? Medications can certainly affect your sleep and some can even cause vivid or frightening dreams. If you are taking a new medication, talk to your provider about the nightmares, this may be the cause. 2. Stress can certainly increase our difficulty with sleep and can also begin to affect our dream states. The dreams may not make much sense, but then again even good dreams don't always make much sense. Ask yourself, do I have any new or renewed stressors in my life? Work, school, relationships, health.... all of these areas and many more are places where stress can hide out. If this is the case, talk with your provider or consider seeing a counselor who may be able to help. 3. Something to consider is that once we start to have anxiety or stress about something, we can begin to obsess about it. My guess is that going to bed for sleep is no longer a pleasant thing for you. Your stress and fear of what may happen when you sleep could start way before you actually go to bed. This could increase your chances of having another bad dream. Try relaxation techniques before going to bed. If you have YouTube, you can pull up "Guided Meditation for Sleep" exercises to help you relax. There are many different ones to choose from. You may also want to try deep breathing.4. There are self-help ideas for managing bad nightmares. If you Google search "Nightmare Rescripting" or "Nightmare Exposure" you may find some ideas and instructions on how to manage dreams. I hope these ideas help. Be well... Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

What makes a healthy marriage last?

What a great question! Marriage (or any long-term committed romantic relationship) is never easy. Ups & downs, doubts and fights are a part of it just the same as the wonderful, tender, blissful moments of connection. Recognizing that hardships are normal and something to work through is a big part of the healthy attitude partners in lasting relationships share. Some degree of conflict is not something to be scared of or a sign it's time to break up as long as all parties involved feel respected. Expressing your needs and wants in a respectful, not accusing manner will increase the chances that your loved one will actually listen, empathize with your perspective and will be more open to finding solutions to your problems together. Working as a team to find solutions to problems you encounter is a much better approach than trying to persuade your partner that you are right, while they are most certainly wrong. Shutting your partner out or allowing resentment and contempt to creep into your relationships is definitely a warning sign that things may not be going the way you want anymore. As long as you both agree that you want to be in that relationship (i.e., are committed to it) and you have a growth mindset ("we will learn from this and grow together to be a better couple in the end"), the foundation of your partnership is strong. What else? Making time for each other, whether it's being playful, having fun or enjoying intimate moments together is also an important part of ensuring a good balance of positive to negative experiences, that will only strenghten your bond. Good luck!

Discussing possible career paths and understanding how to set realistic goals would greatly assist me in achieving self-fulfillment professionally.

In order to gain clarity and guidance regarding your professional goals, it could be helpful for you to explore different career options. Start by reflecting on your interests, strengths, and values. Consider what activities bring you joy and fulfillment, as well as the skills you possess or would like to develop further.

Researching various industries and job roles can also provide valuable insights. Look into different careers that align with your interests and skills, and try to gather information about the day-to-day responsibilities, required qualifications, and potential growth opportunities within those fields. Online resources, such as career websites and professional networking platforms, can be a good starting point for this exploration.

Additionally, seeking out informational interviews or shadow experiences in fields of interest can give you a firsthand understanding of what it's like to work in different industries. Connect with professionals who are already working in areas that intrigue you, and ask if they would be open to sharing their experiences and advice. Hearing different perspectives can help you assess whether certain careers are a good fit for you.

When it comes to making informed decisions, setting realistic goals is crucial. Break down your long-term aspirations into smaller, actionable steps. For each goal, consider the specific skills, knowledge, or experiences you may need to acquire in order to achieve it. Then, create a timeline or action plan outlining how you can work towards these goals incrementally. Remember, progress doesn't have to be linear - setbacks and detours are often part of the journey, so be kind to yourself along the way.

It's understandable that missing out on a promotion opportunity due to lacking essential skills has caused frustration and doubt. However, it's important not to let this define your worth or potential. Instead, view it as an opportunity for growth and self-improvement. Take time to identify the skills you believe are necessary for your desired career path, and actively seek opportunities to develop them. This could include taking online courses, attending workshops, or seeking mentorship from individuals working in your desired field.

Lastly, don't forget to prioritize self-care throughout this process. Managing anxiety and uncertainty can be challenging, especially when it comes to long-term career decisions. Engage in activities that help you relax and recharge, such as exercise, spending time with loved ones, or practicing mindfulness techniques. Surround yourself with a supportive network of friends and family who can offer encouragement and perspective during times of doubt.

Remember, finding clarity in your career path takes time and exploration. Be patient with yourself and embrace the journey of discovering what truly fulfills you professionally.

We went out on two dates, and then despite her original plans on how to pace and conduct the relationship, I ended up at her house on a the Friday night one week after our first date. We respectfully tried not to have sex, but after hours of trying to resist each other, we gave in and we had sex. After that, I slept at her house every night for almost two weeks. Then one day, she went to her family’s house on Thanksgiving and everything changed. Within the short time we were together, we got so close and serious really fast. We had finally found each other. We told each other that we loved each other all the time, even while we were making love. A few days after Thanksgiving, she told me that we would have to go back to her original plans of seeing each other much less frequently. I was very hurt and didn’t understand. Then another week later, she told me she couldn’t do it at all anymore. I was crushed!
   A few days later, she tells me how much she’s missing me and “let’s get together for lunch” or something like that. Then about two weeks later, we finally get together one night and we were so hot for each other (in love, not just sex), but she confessed that the reason for the sudden distance was that the father of her very young child told her he wants to get back together and this totally messed with her. So for her child’s sake, she is now considering the possibility of allowing that to happen. She had told me all about him previously, and it is definite that she has little to no attraction to him, but she would do this putting herself in misery again for her child. Our love for each other is fully established and acknowledged, but she is torn and confused. She doesn’t even think it would work between them as she had to kick him out before for not fulfilling his role properly. I know she needs time, and all I can do is take care of myself. Make sure that you lean on friends and family at this time - we need all the support that we can get when we are heartbroken.

They may use different therapeutic approaches based on your individual needs, but some common ones for depression include cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and psychodynamic therapy.

My boyfriend can't get over my promiscuous past. He says he loves me but says the thought of my past is disgusting and a sexual distraction. He says he should have had more sex with different people. I don't know how to handle this.

I am sorry to hear of your relationship struggles. One thing I wonder is did you volunteer the information about your past or is this something that he asked about? In the future, it is probably best to leave details out of conversations like this. I think it is common and natural for partners to ask about the sexual history. For one thing, it is a good idea to be checked for STD’s before entering into a sexual relationship with someone, and it is fair to share that information with each other. Partners usually want to know how many you have been with and what kind of sexual preferences you have or if there is anything you don’t like to do. This gets into a gray area for some people. I don’t necessarily want to know how many people my partner has been with and I certainly don’t want a whole lot of details. Sometimes that is an image I just don’t want in my head about my partner. Vague details are usually enough.However, I understand that your partner has the details and is not happy with your past. This is a reflection on him, not you. This shows insecurities on his part. You cannot control how he will react to information that you provide to him and you cannot control how he feels about the information. The past should remain in the past and not be held against you in the present or future. If he cannot handle your past then it is going to cloud your relationship. You can offer couples counseling to him and see if he will go with you. I have seen relationships recover from some very serious problems such as infidelity. It takes two people who both want it to work to make it work though. If your boyfriend cannot get over your past, you may have to let him go. Don’t keep yourself tied to someone who is not right for you. Constantly holding your past over your head and holding that against you is only going to bring you down and eventually you may start having insecurities or low self-esteem due to this type of treatment. I don’t see that you have done anything wrong. If you aren’t cheating on him now and you answered his questions about your past honestly, how he handles that information is on him. Ultimately, relationships have a tendency to come and go. Don’t fight to hold onto someone who is not right for you. It is okay to be single and enjoy being the best you that you can be. In time, the right person for you will enter your life.

It takes me a long time to fall asleep; I’d estimate about two hours. I often have nightmares, starting with being eaten by a monster, and I often wake up frightened and unable to breathe. I believe I started losing sleep after breaking up with a girlfriend of 8 years. Also, my father’s business went bankrupt and my mother has a chronic condition. I was under a lot of stress, and life lost meaning. After improving my life and developing a habit of running and exercise to release stress, my symptoms improved. However in the past couple months, I started losing sleep again and having nightmares without warning. How can I solve this issue?

First of all, exercise is always beneficial for your physical and emotional health. That's great that you have added this in your routine. Have you also considered altering your diet? Certain foods are linked with poor sleep. For example, alcohol, caffeine, nicotine and high fat content foods do not bode well with quality sleep, especially right before bed time.  On the other hand, warm milk and foods high in carbohydrates have actually shown to positively impact sleep.Additionally, at bed time it's important to keep your room dim, cool and without distractions (i.e. TV, IPad, Phone). Stick to a sleep routine and avoid any activities close to bed time that demand a lot of attention and energy.As far as your nightmares, there could be many causes contributing to them. Certain foods (many of the ones mentioned) or medications could be the culprit. Doing a bit of research into the ones you are consuming may help you eliminate the offender. You may also benefit from talk therapy with a qualified therapist to discuss any underlying issues you are experiencing. Oftentimes, depression and anxiety can manifest themselves during sleep, causing nightmares. Finally, Yoga has shown to be very beneficial for quality sleep. There are many instructional videos available that can introduce you to the practice if you'd rather not join a class right away. Best of luck to you and I sincerely hope you are able to catch up on some well deserved Z's!

Betrayal in a relationship can be one of the most difficult things a relationship can sustain. Sometimes feelings about the betrayal may also trigger past wounds. It's important to remember that these emotions are valid, but they don't define your worth or determine what lies ahead for you.

One suggestion I have is to focus on self-care during this time. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and fulfillment can help improve your mood and overall well-being. This could include hobbies, exercise, spending time with loved ones, or exploring new interests. Taking care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally is crucial in navigating through difficult times.

Additionally, it might be helpful to explore new opportunities or consider alternative career paths. Networking, updating your resume, and seeking out job search resources can all contribute to increasing your chances of finding a new job.

Regarding your dysfunctional family environment, it's not uncommon for past experiences to have a lasting impact on our mental health. However, it's important to recognize that you have the power to break free from those patterns and create a healthier and more supportive environment for yourself. Seeking therapy or counseling can be beneficial in addressing any unresolved issues from your past and developing coping strategies to improve your mental well-being.

Remember, you are not alone in this journey. Reach out to friends, family, or support groups who can offer understanding and encouragement. Building a strong support system can make a significant difference in managing depression and improving your overall outlook on life.

Lastly, try to practice self-compassion and patience with yourself as you navigate through these challenges. Recovery takes time, and setbacks are normal. Celebrate even the smallest victories along the way and remind yourself that you are deserving of happiness and a fulfilling future.

I hope these suggestions provide some guidance and support as you work towards improving your mental well-being.

Depression has been weighing me down for several months now. I frequently experience feelings of sadness, worthlessness, and low energy. Everyday activities that used to bring me joy no longer hold any interest; I just go through the motions without enthusiasm. It's even becoming hard to concentrate on tasks or make decisions. I'd love to find a way to overcome this apathy and regain my zest for life.

Feeling weighed down by depression is undoubtedly a difficult experience. It's unfortunate that you've been struggling with feelings of sadness, worthlessness, and low energy for such an extended period of time. The loss of interest in activities that previously brought you joy can be disheartening. I understand how challenging it must be to go through the motions without enthusiasm and struggle with concentration and decision-making.

While everyone's journey towards healing is unique, there are some steps you can take to potentially alleviate your symptoms and gradually regain your zest for life:

1. Prioritize self-care: Start by focusing on taking care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally. Make sure you're getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and engaging in regular exercise or physical activity. Maintaining a routine and incorporating relaxation techniques like deep breathing or mindfulness can also be beneficial.

2. Reach out for support: Consider confiding in someone you trust, such as a close friend or family member, about what you're going through. Opening up to them may help lighten the burden and provide emotional support. Additionally, seeking professional help from a therapist or counselor specializing in mental health could offer valuable guidance tailored to your specific needs.

3. Engage in pleasurable activities: Though it may seem difficult at first, try to engage in activities that once brought you happiness. Even if you don't feel immediate enjoyment, participating in these activities consistently might gradually reignite your passion and interest over time.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Depression often leads to negative thinking patterns. Whenever you catch yourself having negative thoughts, try questioning their validity and replacing them with more positive, realistic ones. This process takes practice but can have a significant impact on reshaping your mindset.

5. Set achievable goals: Start with small, achievable goals that contribute to your overall well-being and growth. As you accomplish each goal, even if they are seemingly insignificant, you will likely feel a sense of accomplishment and empowerment.

6. Consider joining a support group: Connecting with others who may be going through similar challenges can provide a sense of belonging and understanding. Support groups offer opportunities to share experiences, learn coping strategies, and gain insights from others who have overcome or are still managing their depression.

Remember, it's important to approach your journey towards healing with patience and kindness toward yourself. Although overcoming apathy and regaining zest for life may take time, taking these steps can potentially help you on the path to recovery.

Whenever I'm faced with uncertainty or unfamiliar situations, anxiety takes hold of me. Simple tasks like going to the grocery store or attending a social gathering cause excessive worry and panic. I start imagining worst-case scenarios and struggle to control my racing thoughts. This anxiety often leads to avoidance behaviors, limiting my opportunities for growth and connection.

It can be challenging when anxiety takes hold of you in uncertain or unfamiliar situations. The excessive worry and panic that arise when faced with simple tasks like going to the grocery store or attending a social gathering can feel overwhelming. It's understandable that imagining worst-case scenarios and struggling to control racing thoughts adds to your distress. This anxiety has also led to avoidance behaviors, which limit your opportunities for growth and connection.

One suggestion I have is to try practicing relaxation techniques when you start feeling anxious. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation can help calm your mind and body. These techniques can be done anywhere and at any time, providing you with a sense of control over your anxiety.

Another strategy that may be helpful is gradually exposing yourself to the situations that trigger your anxiety. Start by breaking down the task into smaller steps and gradually work your way up to more challenging situations. For example, if going to the grocery store causes anxiety, you could begin by visiting during less crowded times or bringing a friend along for support. Over time, as you become more comfortable, you can increase the difficulty level.

It might also be beneficial to challenge the negative thoughts and worst-case scenarios that come to mind. What are some difficulties that a counselor can encounter when dealing with a client?

Although many clients have the capacity to be engaged in the therapeutic process and express their thoughts and feelings in an articulate way, others may demonstrate resistance to treatment which can manifest in ways such as reflecting the desire to end therapy prematurely, cancelling appointments, or arriving late. A resistant client can also make the process of the therapist engaging the client, challenging.Once the therapist identifies the resistance, it is essential for the  therapist to address it with the the client and encourage the client to focus on the therapeutic goals.In my experience, I have observed that people have many reasons why they begin to show resistance. Some may believe the therapist is judgmental and they may not for one reason or another, feel  emotionally safe with the therapist. Others may not feel comfortable talking about their feelings, and it may appear that they never developed a rapport with the therapist.Sometimes a person may harbor feelings of distrust, or dislike for the therapist which eventually creates barriers to good treatment outcomes.

I experience intense feelings of loneliness during these episodes, and it's affecting my overall mood and self-esteem.

In terms of coping strategies, I've tried joining different clubs or organizations to meet new people, but I often find myself holding back and not fully engaging in social interactions. Additionally, I find comfort in spending time alone and pursuing solitary hobbies, such as reading or painting. However, while these activities provide temporary relief, they don't address the underlying issue of my lack of meaningful connections.

It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of frustration and disappointment when it comes to your social relationships, and I can understand why it's been such a challenging issue for you. Trusting others after going through a betrayal can be incredibly difficult and can make it harder to form close friendships.

Therapy can definitely help you work through these feelings and develop healthier social relationships. One technique that we can explore is called cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on identifying negative thought patterns and replacing them with more positive and realistic ones. We can work together to challenge the belief that everyone will betray you or spread personal information, helping you build a more balanced perspective on trust.

Another approach that might be helpful is developing effective communication skills. Learning how to express your thoughts and emotions assertively can increase your confidence in social situations and improve the chances of building meaningful connections. We can practice different techniques during our sessions, such as active listening, expressing boundaries, and asserting your needs in a constructive way.

In addition to therapy, there are some exercises you can try on your own to start overcoming your fear of vulnerability. One exercise is journaling about your past experiences with trust and betrayal. By reflecting on these events and writing down your thoughts and feelings, you may gain insight into any patterns that have developed over time. This reflection can also help you identify any beliefs or fears that might be holding you back from trusting others.

It could also be beneficial for you to gradually expose yourself to social situations that feel uncomfortable but manageable. Start by attending smaller gatherings or get-togethers where you feel less pressure to open up right away. With time and repeated positive experiences, you may find that your fear of vulnerability decreases, allowing for more authentic connections to form.

Remember that progress takes time, so be patient with yourself throughout this process. It's important to celebrate small victories along the way, even if they may seem insignificant at first. Therapy can provide you with the support, guidance, and tools to work through these challenges, but ultimately, it will be up to you to implement what you learn and push yourself out of your comfort zone.

"Lately, I've been experiencing intense anxiety in social situations. Even the thought of attending social events makes me feel extremely anxious and overwhelmed. This has caused me to isolate myself from others, which is making me feel even more lonely. My goal is to learn effective coping mechanisms to manage my anxiety and regain my ability to engage with others."

It's commendable that you're taking the initiative to find effective coping mechanisms for your anxiety and work towards engaging with others again. If social situations have been causing intense anxiety for you, it might be helpful to start by gradually exposing yourself to them.

One approach you could try is called exposure therapy. This involves gradually exposing yourself to social situations that cause anxiety while incorporating relaxation techniques. For example, you can start by attending smaller events or gatherings where you feel more comfortable, and as you become more at ease, build up to bigger ones. While doing this, remember to practice deep breathing exercises or grounding techniques to help manage any overwhelming feelings.

Another technique you may find beneficial is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. By recognizing and replacing these thoughts with more realistic and positive ones, you can begin to shift your perspective and reduce your anxiety levels in social situations.

Additionally, self-care plays a crucial role in managing anxiety. Taking care of your physical and emotional well-being can greatly impact your overall mental health. Prioritize activities and practices that bring you joy, whether it's exercising, pursuing hobbies, connecting with loved ones, or practicing mindfulness and relaxation techniques such as meditation or yoga.

If you feel comfortable, reaching out to trustworthy friends or family members about what you've been going through may provide support and understanding. Sometimes, having someone by your side during social events can offer comfort and encouragement. Building a strong support system can also include seeking out local groups or communities with similar interests where you can meet like-minded individuals and gradually expand your social network.

Remember to be patient with yourself throughout this process. Overcoming anxiety takes time, and setbacks are normal. Celebrate each step forward, no matter how small, and don't hesitate to seek professional help if you ever feel overwhelmed or need extra support along the way.

Anxiety has become overwhelming, and I need guidance on how to regain a sense of calmness. Every day, almost every hour even, I experience intrusive thoughts that spiral into worst-case scenarios. For instance, when I hear sirens outside, my mind immediately jumps to the conclusion that something terrible has happened to my loved ones. These constant worries eat away at me, leaving me exhausted and seeking techniques to manage this anxiety.

One helpful technique for managing anxiety is called grounding. Grounding techniques can help bring you back to the present moment and provide a sense of calmness. One popular grounding technique is called 5-4-3-2-1. 

Here's how it works: 
- Take a deep breath, then look around and identify five things you can see in your immediate environment. It could be anything from the color of the walls to an object on your desk.
- Next, try to name four things you can physically feel. This could be the texture of your clothing against your skin or the sensation of your feet touching the ground.
- Then, focus on three things you can hear. It may be the sound of birds chirping outside, the hum of the air conditioning, or even your own breathing.
- After that, think about two things you can smell. It could be the scent of a candle, coffee brewing, or freshly cut grass.
- Lastly, notice one thing you can taste. It might be the lingering flavor of your last meal or a sip of water.

By going through this exercise, you are redirecting your attention away from intrusive thoughts and bringing yourself into the present moment. With practice, this technique can become more natural and effective in calming your anxious mind.

Another useful strategy for managing anxiety is incorporating relaxation exercises into your routine. Deep breathing exercises, such as diaphragmatic breathing or belly breathing, can activate your body's natural relaxation response. You can start by finding a quiet and comfortable space. Close your eyes and take a slow, deep breath in through your nose, allowing your belly to expand. Hold your breath for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth, letting go of any tension or stress. Repeat this process several times, focusing solely on your breath.

Additionally, engaging in regular physical activity has been shown to reduce anxiety symptoms. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Find an activity that you enjoy and make it a habit to incorporate into your daily routine. It could be walking, dancing, swimming, or any other form of exercise that gets your body moving.

Incorporating relaxation techniques like mindfulness meditation can also help alleviate anxiety. Mindfulness involves focusing your attention on the present moment without judgment. There are many guided mindfulness meditations available online or through mobile apps that can assist you in developing this skill. 

Remember, managing anxiety is not about eliminating all worries, but rather finding healthy ways to cope with them. By incorporating grounding exercises, relaxation techniques, regular physical activity, and mindfulness into your routine, you can regain a sense of calmness and reduce the impact of intrusive thoughts.

In chess, why is the queen valued at nine points instead of eight?

In chess, typically chess pieces are valued based on their importance. 
For example, 
Pawn - 1 point 
Knight - 3 points
Bishop - 3 points
Rook - 5 points
Queen - 9 points

Since the queen can move like the bishop and the rook, simple math would suggest that it is valued at 8 points (3 + 5). 
However, the game of chess, involves complex scenarios and strategies and having a single piece that can move in all directions gives it a distinct advantage during various phases of the chess game. 
This is why the queen is given a higher point valuation.

Depression is very common. Research suggests that one in three people may experience it in their lifetime and at any one point, ten percent of adults may be experiencing it.  Most therapists are very good at spotting the signs and treating accordingly, although only a physician can prescribe medication.The great news is that depression is treatable. Some people experiencing depression may benefit from medication (often to lift the heaviness of the illness enough so that one can focus on psychotherapy), and therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy and behavioural activation therapy have demonstrated a clear ability to reduce symptoms of depression.
